standard: Modified Wells rule (low Wells score with negative D-dimer to avoid ultrasound); re-audit against the local revised diagnostic algorithm; no target stated
finding: 510 (96.9%) had D-dimer and ultrasound results; 265 (51.9%) negative D-dimer, of whom 143 (53.9%) had a low Wells score. 7 of 143 with negative D-dimer and low Wells score had a DVT, all with a risk factor not in the Wells score; none without risk factors had a DVT (NPV 100%).
change: Revised clinical diagnostic algorithm adding assessment of extra risk factors to the Wells score; ultrasound omitted in patients with negative D-dimer, low Wells score and no risk factors.
setting: Royal London Hospital, nurse-led Fast Response Team outpatient clinic for suspected lower limb DVT
cycle1_result: 510 (96.9%) had D-dimer and ultrasound results; 265 (51.9%) negative D-dimer, of whom 143 (53.9%) had a low Wells score. 7 of 143 with negative D-dimer and low Wells score had a DVT, all with a risk factor not in the Wells score; none without risk factors had a DVT (NPV 100%).
intervention: Revised clinical diagnostic algorithm adding assessment of extra risk factors to the Wells score; ultrasound omitted in patients with negative D-dimer, low Wells score and no risk factors.
cycle2_result: All 290 (100%) had complete results; 94 (32.4%) negative D-dimer, 43 with low Wells score, of whom 30 had risk factors and were scanned. 1/94 (1%) with negative D-dimer had a DVT (on OCP). 13 of 290 (4.5%) not scanned under the algorithm; all negative D-dimer patients had probability score and risk factors recorded.
other_findings: The D-dimer assay changed between cycles, lowering the proportion of negative results. The re-audit saved £767.

finding: Whole 2003-2011 cohort n=471,590. Before NHFD: early surgery fairly stable (annual RR 0.987, 1.3% relative decrease per year); 30-day mortality fell from 11.5% to 10.9% (1.8% relative reduction per year).

cycle1_result: Whole 2003-2011 cohort n=471,590. Before NHFD: early surgery fairly stable (annual RR 0.987, 1.3% relative decrease per year); 30-day mortality fell from 11.5% to 10.9% (1.8% relative reduction per year).

change: Multidisciplinary Rapid Recovery Group with parallel PDSA cycles: ropivacaine local infiltration protocol, oxycodone MR, preprinted drug charts, Taurus frames and nurse-led mobilisation, stopping routine MSU and TED stockings, and a ring-fenced elective ward.
setting: North Devon District Hospital, elective hip and knee replacement pathway
cycle1_result: Mean length of stay 3.6 days for both total hip and total knee replacement; Model Hospital median length of stay 4.2 days (hips, 41st nationally) and 3.9 days (knees, 34th).
intervention: Multidisciplinary Rapid Recovery Group with parallel PDSA cycles: ropivacaine local infiltration protocol, oxycodone MR, preprinted drug charts, Taurus frames and nurse-led mobilisation, stopping routine MSU and TED stockings, and a ring-fenced elective ward.

topic: Elective cancellations due to asymptomatic bacteriuria
title: Introduction of a New Protocol to Limit the Number of Cancelled Elective Orthopaedic Operations Due to Asymptomatic Bacteriuria.
standard: not reported
finding: Of 33 all-cause cancellations, 7 (21.2%) were cancelled for UTI risk on positive urinalysis; only 1 (14.3%) of these was symptomatic, so 6 (85.7%) were cancelled for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
change: New symptom-based protocol from 1 May 2019: all patients complete a 7-item UTI symptom questionnaire and surgery is cancelled only if two or more symptoms are reported, regardless of urinalysis.
setting: Lister Hospital, Stevenage (East & North Herts NHS Trust), large district general hospital offering tertiary orthopaedic services; cancelled elective orthopaedic operations
cycle1_result: Of 33 all-cause cancellations, 7 (21.2%) were cancelled for UTI risk on positive urinalysis; only 1 (14.3%) of these was symptomatic, so 6 (85.7%) were cancelled for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
intervention: New symptom-based protocol from 1 May 2019: all patients complete a 7-item UTI symptom questionnaire and surgery is cancelled only if two or more symptoms are reported, regardless of urinalysis.
cycle2_result: Of 45 all-cause cancellations, 2 (4.4%) were cancelled for UTI risk, both symptomatic; 4 (8.8%) had positive urinalysis, the 2 asymptomatic ones cancelled for unrelated reasons. No cancellations for asymptomatic bacteriuria; estimated 71.4% reduction in cancellations for UTI risk.
other_findings: Patients with positive urinalysis whose operations were not cancelled were not captured, so the true effect is estimated. Each cancelled operation was estimated to waste 2.1 hours of theatre time (about £2,525).

title: Introducing a new proforma for the safe use of intraoperative tourniquets in orthopaedic surgery.
standard: BOAST 'The Safe Use of Intraoperative Tourniquets': document exsanguination method, isolation method, skin condition, pressure and duration; pressure lower limb SBP + 70–130 mmHg, upper limb SBP + 50–100 mmHg; duration ideally < 120 min
finding: Exsanguination method documented 5.6%, isolation (shut-off drape) 2.4%, skin condition 0%; duration not in operative note 23.0%, not recorded at all 1.6%; > 120 min in 1.6%; pressure within standard in 24.3% lower limb, 34.8% upper limb and 66.7% paediatric cases.
change: Local presentation at trust Quality & Safety Half Day and 'PRESSURE' mnemonic posters in theatres and offices, followed by a new electronic patient record with a tourniquet section and BOAST-based auto-text proforma in the operation note.
setting: Ashford and St Peter's Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust; trauma and elective orthopaedic surgery across both sites
cycle1_result: Exsanguination method documented 5.6%, isolation (shut-off drape) 2.4%, skin condition 0%; duration not in operative note 23.0%, not recorded at all 1.6%; > 120 min in 1.6%; pressure within standard in 24.3% lower limb, 34.8% upper limb and 66.7% paediatric cases.
intervention: Local presentation at trust Quality & Safety Half Day and 'PRESSURE' mnemonic posters in theatres and offices, followed by a new electronic patient record with a tourniquet section and BOAST-based auto-text proforma in the operation note.
cycle2_result: Exsanguination method documented 42.9% (p = 0.001), isolation 42.9% (p = 0.0001), skin condition 64.3% (p = 0.0001); duration not in operative note 10.2% (p = 0.0269), not recorded 0%; none > 120 min; pressure within standard 13.0% lower limb, 35.7% upper limb, 14.2% paediatric (no significant change).
other_findings: An interim re-audit in March 2022 after education alone (n = 153) showed little change (e.g. exsanguination 9.8%, skin condition 5.2%). Staff survey (n = 19) found over 50% sized tourniquets on 'whatever looks the best fit' and 31.6% did not know paediatric pressures.

topic: Native hip dislocation time to reduction
title: Traumatic Native Hip Dislocations: An Audit at a Major Trauma Centre and Assessment of Clinical Practice at Centres Across the United Kingdom.
standard: No formal standard; practice measured against reduction within 6 hours and 12 hours of injury, based on published research
finding: Mean time to reduction 532 minutes (240–804); 4 (29%) reduced within 6 hours and 11 (79%) within 12 hours (abstract gives 28.6% and 71.4%). ED reductions (n=2) mean 275 minutes vs theatre (n=13) 576 minutes.
setting: Major trauma centre, University Hospital of Wales, Cardiff; plus survey of Welsh EDs and UK MTCs
cycle1_result: Mean time to reduction 532 minutes (240–804); 4 (29%) reduced within 6 hours and 11 (79%) within 12 hours (abstract gives 28.6% and 71.4%). ED reductions (n=2) mean 275 minutes vs theatre (n=13) 576 minutes.
other_findings: Post-reduction neurovascular status documented in 100% and post-reduction CT in 87%; one AVN and one chondrolysis. title: Creating Novel Standards for Datapoints on an Elective Orthopaedic Theatre List Document.
standard: No existing standard; locally defined datapoints (surgical team, anaesthesia type, side, prosthesis/equipment, fluoroscopy, acronyms, extra patient information), later adopted as the 'William Harvey theatre list standard'
finding: 115 lists, 326 cases. Consultant in charge recorded in 85%; lead anaesthetist missing in 4.3%; 98% listed as GA (spinal 0.3%); 76.8% had no prosthesis/equipment detail; fluoroscopy requirement stated in 11% of cases needing it; acronyms used in 28%; extra patient information in 6%.
change: Proforma of essential information for waiting list coordinators, minor IT changes to the theatre list input form, and education of waiting list coordinators and trainees.
setting: Elective orthopaedic theatre lists (excluding spine and trauma), William Harvey Hospital, Ashford
cycle1_result: 115 lists, 326 cases. Consultant in charge recorded in 85%; lead anaesthetist missing in 4.3%; 98% listed as GA (spinal 0.3%); 76.8% had no prosthesis/equipment detail; fluoroscopy requirement stated in 11% of cases needing it; acronyms used in 28%; extra patient information in 6%.
intervention: Proforma of essential information for waiting list coordinators, minor IT changes to the theatre list input form, and education of waiting list coordinators and trainees.
cycle2_result: 100 lists, 255 cases. Consultant in charge recorded in 100%; 80% listed as GA (14.5% spinal per abstract; 37 regional); no prosthesis/equipment detail fell to 43% (abstract: prosthesis/equipment mentioned 34% vs 23%); fluoroscopy stated in 25% of cases needing it; acronyms 6%; extra patient information 49.8%.

finding: Full adherence 3 (6.0%), partial 16 (32.0%), overall compliance 38.0%; not adhered 31 (62.0%).

title: Perioperative pain management intervention in older patients with hip fracture in an orthogeriatric unit. A controlled before/after study assessing an audit and feedback intervention (PAIN-AGE).

setting: Orthogeriatric unit (experimental) versus conventional orthopaedic unit (control), Grenoble Alpes University Hospital; controlled before/after audit and feedback study
cycle1_period: December 2018 to April 2019 (before intervention, started May 2019)
cycle1_result: Postoperative 3 g/day acetaminophen 16% (16/99); preoperative 9%; nurse adherence to acetaminophen prescriptions 13% preoperatively and 13% postoperatively.
intervention: Audit and feedback with nurses: two 1-hour pain teaching sessions, distribution of a pain assessment scale, protocol updated to 'give acetaminophen regardless of pain assessment', medicine staffing reviewed with clinical pharmacy, and night/weekend standby with a Saturday ward round.

title: Understanding Barriers to Early Rehabilitation Following the Surgery for Fragility Hip Fractures: A Single-Centre Audit.
standard: National guidelines (NICE): mobilisation on the day of or the day after hip fracture surgery; two hours of physiotherapy in the first week after surgery; no target stated
finding: 93% (106/113) seen by a physiotherapist on the day of or day after surgery (main orthopaedic ward 94%, 80/85; outliers 93%, 21/28; P=0.3). 40% (46/113) had delayed mobilisation. 83% (94/113) had two hours of physiotherapy in the first week. Clear documentation of mobilisation in 85% (97/113).
setting: Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother Hospital, Margate, Kent; main orthopaedic ward and outlier wards
cycle1_result: 93% (106/113) seen by a physiotherapist on the day of or day after surgery (main orthopaedic ward 94%, 80/85; outliers 93%, 21/28; P=0.3). 40% (46/113) had delayed mobilisation. 83% (94/113) had two hours of physiotherapy in the first week. Clear documentation of mobilisation in 85% (97/113).
other_findings: Reasons for delayed mobilisation: post-operative delirium 32.6% (15/46), low haemoglobin 26% (12/46), pain 21.7% (10/46), dementia 4.3% (2/46), no documented reason 15.2% (7/46). Presence of one or more of these factors was associated with one-year mortality of 25.8% (16/62, P=0.05), with delirium the strongest single factor (P=0.01).
authors: Al-Dahan T; Murhekar S; Abed M; Shinde K

standard: NICE CG124 Section 1.6 (choice of arthroplasty, THR for eligible displaced intracapsular fractures, extramedullary implants for A1/A2 trochanteric fractures, intramedullary nail for subtrochanteric fractures)
finding: Overall compliance 76.04% (1244/1636). THR documented as considered in 43.6% (193/443) of eligible patients; 56.43% of THR-indicated patients had no documented consideration (65.41% in 2020).
change: A 'smart phrase' NICE THR-eligibility checklist added to the electronic (Epic) neck of femur clerking proforma in June 2021.
setting: Addenbrooke's Hospital, Cambridge (major trauma centre), patients over 65 having hip fracture surgery
cycle1_result: Overall compliance 76.04% (1244/1636). THR documented as considered in 43.6% (193/443) of eligible patients; 56.43% of THR-indicated patients had no documented consideration (65.41% in 2020).
intervention: A 'smart phrase' NICE THR-eligibility checklist added to the electronic (Epic) neck of femur clerking proforma in June 2021.

title: Oral Nutritional Supplementation in Older Adults with a Hip Fracture-Findings from a Bi-National Clinical Audit.
standard: ESPEN guideline and ANZ Hip Fracture Clinical Care Standard: all older adults with hip fracture should be offered oral nutritional supplements regardless of nutritional status
finding: ONS provided or prescribed for 182/385 (47.3%) of older adults having hip fracture surgery. ONS was more likely if malnourished on formal testing (OR 11.92; 95% CI 6.57, 21.69).
setting: 29 hospitals (24 Australian, 5 New Zealand) taking part in the ANZ Hip Fracture Registry Nutrition Sprint Audit
cycle1_result: ONS provided or prescribed for 182/385 (47.3%) of older adults having hip fracture surgery. ONS was more likely if malnourished on formal testing (OR 11.92; 95% CI 6.57, 21.69).
other_findings: ONS was also more likely with no preoperative medical assessment (OR 2.26), cognitive impairment (OR 1.83) and severe frailty or terminal illness (OR 3.17); New Zealand patients were less likely to receive ONS (OR 0.45). 30.9% of patients were diagnosed as malnourished.

cycle1_result: ED: 0% splint (all back slab). Fracture clinic: 62 (95.4%) full cast, 3 (4.6%) splint. Discharged at first visit 5 (7.7%); second visit 56 (86.2%); third visit 4 (6.2%).

change: Teaching sessions, MDT meetings and bedside teaching; local protocol flowcharts; push to start antiresorptives before discharge; new orthogeriatrics SHO role; new older people osteoporosis clinic
setting: Warrington Hospital, district general hospital; inpatients aged 65 and over with fragility fractures
cycle1_result: Inpatient bisphosphonates started in 23/144 (16%); 105/121 (87%) not started by GP after discharge; FRAX recorded in 78/144 (54%); vitamin D assessed in 89/144 (62%) and replaced in 78/144 (54%); 110/144 no DEXA scan; 34/144 (25%) referred to metabolic bone clinic

finding: 39% of non-operative patients triaged to the VFC within 24 hours; 61% sent directly to face-to-face clinic. 35,399 face-to-face fracture clinic appointments (also given as 35,339 in the results).
change: COVID-19-era policy changes: mandatory VFC triage of all non-operative injuries via a smartphone referral app with daily consultant-led multidisciplinary review, and an early appropriate discharge / patient-initiated follow-up policy; national lockdowns also occurred.
setting: University teaching hospital and regional trauma and orthopaedic referral centre serving four peripheral sites (Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital, Drogheda, per affiliation); non-operative fracture pathway
cycle1_result: 39% of non-operative patients triaged to the VFC within 24 hours; 61% sent directly to face-to-face clinic. 35,399 face-to-face fracture clinic appointments (also given as 35,339 in the results).

change: Three PDSA cycles (July 2023 to January 2024): CES working group and trust-level awareness; new locally adapted SOP based on the GIRFT pathway with CES-specific shorter MRI sequences; ED triage and assessment posters, board round, grand round and senior-led teaching. Planned extension of MRI hours was not achieved.
setting: Medway Maritime Hospital, Gillingham; district general hospital emergency department without on-site emergency spinal surgery
cycle1_result: Median time from ED presentation to MRI 5.9 hours (IQR 4.9–14.7) although median MRI request to scan was 1.7 hours (IQR 1.1–3.7), meeting the GIRFT target; 8% of patients incorrectly sent to the GP-led MEDOCC service. At PDSA 1: 38% of MRIs unnecessary, 0.5 CES MRIs/day, time to analgesia 5.3 hours (IQR 3.8–7.0), 9% inappropriately triaged to MEDOCC.
intervention: Three PDSA cycles (July 2023 to January 2024): CES working group and trust-level awareness; new locally adapted SOP based on the GIRFT pathway with CES-specific shorter MRI sequences; ED triage and assessment posters, board round, grand round and senior-led teaching. cycle1_result: Criterion 1 (fibula superimposed by posterior tibia) 83%; criterion 2 (talar domes superimposed) 61%; criterion 3 (open uniform tibiotalar joint) 69%; criterion 4 (landmarks included) 99%.

topic: Soft tissue knee injury pathway timescales and MRI use
title: A Retrospective Audit of the Timescales Involved in the Diagnosis and Management of Soft Tissue Knee Injuries at a Single National Health Service Trust: A Quality Service Improvement and Redesign Project.
standard: NHS Constitution RTT standard (92% of consultant-led pathways completed within 18 weeks); Diagnostics DM01 standard (<1% waiting over six weeks for MRI); BOA/BOAST and regional MSK guidance of MRI within two weeks where diagnosis uncertain, with review within 7-14 days; NICE CKS and EBI guidance on selective MRI
finding: MRI utilisation 77.7% (269/346). Median waits: presentation to knee clinic 7 days, MRI referral to scan 33 days, scan to review 22 days; median presentation to diagnosis 60 days and to definitive management 97 days. 58.0% waited over four weeks for MRI; only 11.9% scanned within one week; 10.3% reviewed within seven days and 26.2% within 14 days. 42.8% of MRIs normal/degenerative.
setting: Acute knee clinic, Ashford and St Peter's Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (single NHS trust)
cycle1_result: MRI utilisation 77.7% (269/346). Median waits: presentation to knee clinic 7 days, MRI referral to scan 33 days, scan to review 22 days; median presentation to diagnosis 60 days and to definitive management 97 days. 58.0% waited over four weeks for MRI; only 11.9% scanned within one week; 10.3% reviewed within seven days and 26.2% within 14 days. 42.8% of MRIs normal/degenerative.
other_findings: Surgery in 11.0% (38/346) with median 128 days from presentation to operation; only 7.2% of non-operative patients started physiotherapy within 30 days of clinic (median 70.5 days). GP referrals had longer median time to diagnosis (74 days) than UTC (53.5) or ED (58); a physiotherapy-first, criteria-based MRI pathway and re-audit were proposed.

cycle1_result: Marker ball present in 27 (45%). Of these, entirely visible 16 (59%) and correctly positioned 11 (41%); overall compliance 59% (n=16).

finding: Tympanic membrane integrity documented in otitis externa 34.3%; nasal fracture reviewed within 7 days 58.3%, MUA within 14 days 92.9%; SSNHL audiogram within 24 hours 33.3%; epistaxis cautery for visible vessel 87.2%, documentation of counselling 28.0%.

cycle1_result: Tympanic membrane integrity documented in otitis externa 34.3%; nasal fracture reviewed within 7 days 58.3%, MUA within 14 days 92.9%; SSNHL audiogram within 24 hours 33.3%; epistaxis cautery for visible vessel 87.2%, documentation of counselling 28.0%.

topic: Hip fracture delirium and cognitive assessment

title: WaSTE: a multicentre audit of waste segregation practices in elective knee and hip arthroplasty.
standard: National waste management guidance: infectious (orange) stream only for suspected infectious agents, otherwise offensive (tiger-stripe) and general streams; no numerical target stated
finding: 92 THAs and 130 TKAs; mean total waste 14.79 kg per THA and 13.61 kg per TKA; infectious waste the largest category (9.88 kg THA, 8.68 kg TKA). Only 5/10 trusts used an offensive waste stream and 8/10 used recycling; significant inter-hospital variation in all waste categories (p < 0.001).
setting: Ten UK NHS trusts, elective primary total hip and knee arthroplasty (prospective multicentre audit)
cycle1_result: 92 THAs and 130 TKAs; mean total waste 14.79 kg per THA and 13.61 kg per TKA; infectious waste the largest category (9.88 kg THA, 8.68 kg TKA). other_findings: On multivariable regression, hospital site was the main predictor of waste; trusts using offensive waste eliminated nearly all infectious waste. Switching streams estimated to save about £1.38 per THA and £1.22 per TKA.

standard: HSE National Consent policy and local guideline: DNAR orders clearly documented in records and communicated at nursing handover and clinical rounds

cycle1_result: 33% of patients with signed DNAR forms did not have DNAR status on the nursing handover sheet; 89% of forms at front of chart, 7% with admission note, 4% unfiled; 6% of staff very confident of DNAR status without notes (24% with access).
intervention: Recommended: keep only original coloured DNAR forms on the ward, file forms at front of charts, add a DNAR status column to medical and nursing handover sheets.

cycle1_result: Of 94 eligible patients (of 247 attendees), 81% (n=77) had a bespoke sticker and 71% of these were completed (n=55). cycle1_result: 99 of 168 patients on antibiotics; Microguide compliance 39-65% (mean 53%); indication and duration on drug charts 89%.

change: Local guidelines amended in 2015 to dose obese children on lean body mass/ideal weight for height and reduce maximum daily dose to 75 mg/kg/day; education of prescribers recommended.
setting: Paediatric surgical inpatients and discharges, Cardiff and Vale UHB
cycle1_result: Weight documented in 84% of inpatient and 94% of discharge prescriptions; height documented for no patient; IV/PO combined prescribing in 32 inpatients; of 52 on IV paracetamol, 20 not reviewed at 48 hours (only 3 appropriate).
intervention: Local guidelines amended in 2015 to dose obese children on lean body mass/ideal weight for height and reduce maximum daily dose to 75 mg/kg/day; education of prescribers recommended.
other_findings: 100 inpatient and 35 discharge prescriptions; overweight/obese children received doses up to 30 mg/kg (oral inpatient) and 33 mg/kg (discharge) based on ideal body weight.
authors: McArtney R; Atkinson A
citation: McArtney R, Atkinson A. AUDIT OF PARACETAMOL PRESCRIPTIONS IN PAEDIATRIC SURGICAL PATIENTS. Arch Dis Child. 2016;101(9):e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.39. PMID: 27540219.

title: THE DEVELOPMENT OF A QUALITY IMPROVEMENT SYSTEM TO MONITOR, ASSESS AND FEEDBACK PRESCRIBING ERRORS IN PAEDIATRIC INTENSIVE CARE.
standard: Local Zero Tolerance prescribing standards
finding: Unit mean error rate 12.5%.
change: Automated individual feedback forms for prescribers, posters and discussion at clinical governance meetings.
setting: Paediatric intensive care unit, Central Manchester University Hospitals
cycle1_result: Unit mean error rate 12.5%.
intervention: Automated individual feedback forms for prescribers, posters and discussion at clinical governance meetings.
other_findings: In 7 prescribers the error rate fell from mean 15.3 to 9.4 (p=0.29, not significant).
authors: Morris S; Rivett C
citation: Morris S, Rivett C. THE DEVELOPMENT OF A QUALITY IMPROVEMENT SYSTEM TO MONITOR, ASSESS AND FEEDBACK PRESCRIBING ERRORS IN PAEDIATRIC INTENSIVE CARE. Arch Dis Child. 2016;101(9):e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.42. PMID: 27540223.

title: CHILDREN'S WARFARIN CLINIC-AN AUDIT OF THE NEW PHARMACIST-LED TELEPHONE SERVICE BASED ON A UNIQUE COMPUTERISED SYSTEM COMPARED TO THE WARD BASED PAPER SYSTEM.
standard: NPSA safety standards for warfarin dosing
finding: Previous ward-based paper system: 44 patients, 1289 INRs; 11 patients (25%) lost to follow-up.
change: Pharmacist-led telephone warfarin service using a computerised documentation system replaced ward-based junior doctor dosing on paper.
setting: Children's warfarin clinic (pharmacist-led telephone service), Leeds Children's Hospital
cycle1_result: Previous ward-based paper system: 44 patients, 1289 INRs; 11 patients (25%) lost to follow-up.
intervention: Pharmacist-led telephone warfarin service using a computerised documentation system replaced ward-based junior doctor dosing on paper.
cycle2_result: 73 patients, 1547 INRs; fully compliant with NPSA standards; no patients lost to follow-up; no significant difference in safety indicators versus the original service.
other_findings: No inappropriate target INRs in either service; 38/53 (72%) parents returned the satisfaction survey and 28 (78%) rated the clinic excellent.
authors: Brooks T; Brown J; Woolley E
citation: Brooks T, Brown J, Woolley E. CHILDREN'S WARFARIN CLINIC-AN AUDIT OF THE NEW PHARMACIST-LED TELEPHONE SERVICE BASED ON A UNIQUE COMPUTERISED SYSTEM COMPARED TO THE WARD BASED PAPER SYSTEM. Arch Dis Child. 2016;101(9):e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.43. PMID: 27540224.

title: AN AUDIT OF VANCOMYCIN PLASMA CONCENTRATIONS WHEN VANCOMYCIN IS ADMINISTERED BY CONTINUOUS INTRAVENOUS INFUSION IN NEONATES.
standard: Desired therapeutic vancomycin plasma concentration 15-25 mg/L
finding: 28% of concentrations within the therapeutic range.
change: Switch to continuous intravenous infusion regimen (loading dose 15 mg/kg then 20-50 mg/kg/day by creatinine and CGA).
setting: Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, Birmingham Women's NHS Foundation Trust
cycle1_period: January to July 2014 (intermittent bolus regimen, retrospective)
cycle1_result: 28% of concentrations within the therapeutic range.
intervention: Switch to continuous intravenous infusion regimen (loading dose 15 mg/kg then 20-50 mg/kg/day by creatinine and CGA).
cycle2_result: 62% of 115 concentrations within range (first 60.8%, second 60%, subsequent 65.6%); 71.3% allowing 10% variability.
other_findings: Another hospital using pharmacy-prepared syringes achieved 77%; authors plan prefilled syringes and a re-audit.
authors: Whitticase L; Holder G; Cawsey M; Bedford-Russell A
citation: Whitticase L, Holder G, Cawsey M, Bedford-Russell A. AN AUDIT OF VANCOMYCIN PLASMA CONCENTRATIONS WHEN VANCOMYCIN IS ADMINISTERED BY CONTINUOUS INTRAVENOUS INFUSION IN NEONATES. Arch Dis Child. 2016;101(9):e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.56. PMID: 27540238.

title: AN AUDIT TO ASSESS THE TIMINGS OF TTAS AND INPATIENT ORDERS IN PAEDIATRICS; FROM WRITING, TO SCREENING, TO DISPENSING, AND TO LEAVING DISPENSARY.
standard: Trust KPI: 85% of urgent items (TTAs) dispensed within 1 hour; 85% of non-urgent items within 3 hrs
finding: TTAs averaged 2 hrs from logging in to checking (n=12, standard 1 hour); inpatient orders averaged 5 hrs 51 minutes to leave dispensary (n=22, standard 3 hrs).
setting: Pharmacy dispensary serving paediatric wards, Barts Health NHS Trust
cycle1_result: TTAs averaged 2 hrs from logging in to checking (n=12, standard 1 hour); inpatient orders averaged 5 hrs 51 minutes to leave dispensary (n=22, standard 3 hrs).
other_findings: Labelling was the rate-limiting step; proposals include extra labelling staff at peak times and induction teaching; re-audit planned in 3 months.
authors: Hale A; Christiansen N; Calvert H
citation: Hale A, Christiansen N, Calvert H. AN AUDIT TO ASSESS THE TIMINGS OF TTAS AND INPATIENT ORDERS IN PAEDIATRICS; FROM WRITING, TO SCREENING, TO DISPENSING, AND TO LEAVING DISPENSARY. Arch Dis Child. 2016;101(9):e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.67. PMID: 27540250.

title: P02 An audit of vancomycin dosing in the neonatal units
standard: Local neonatal vancomycin guideline; 100% adherence
finding: Correct initial dose 28/28 (100%); level taken at correct time 13/15 (87%); 19/31 levels (62%) within 10–20 mg/L; all 6 levels >20 mg/L had next dose held, but follow-up adjustment often suboptimal; 3 of 4 low levels not acted on.
change: Guideline amended (single safe range 10–20 mg/L, doses adjusted on levels not age) and teaching sessions with worked examples planned for prescribers and nurses.
setting: Neonatal units
cycle1_result: Correct initial dose 28/28 (100%); level taken at correct time 13/15 (87%); 19/31 levels (62%) within 10–20 mg/L; all 6 levels >20 mg/L had next dose held, but follow-up adjustment often suboptimal; 3 of 4 low levels not acted on.
intervention: Guideline amended (single safe range 10–20 mg/L, doses adjusted on levels not age) and teaching sessions with worked examples planned for prescribers and nurses.
other_findings: 19 patients had 28 courses and 31 levels. Levels appeared to be interpreted in isolation, causing avoidable repeat high levels.
authors: Penny F; Shruti P
citation: Penny F, Shruti P. P02 An audit of vancomycin dosing in the neonatal units. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e1.5-e1. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.13.

title: P26 An audit of the use of amikacin for early onset sepsis in premature neonates in an inpatient neonatal unit
standard: Trust Neonatal Infection Guideline: 100% adherence to criteria, amikacin 15 mg/kg, level at 24 hours before second dose, further doses only if level <5 mg/L or on pharmacist advice
finding: 100% adhered to guideline criteria and 100% prescribed 15 mg/kg; 12 (24%) had no level at 24 hours; of 38 with 24-hour levels only 6 (16%) were <5 mg/L; 17/23 (74%) in range at 36 hours; 2 patients received doses despite levels >5 mg/L.
change: Recommended change from 24-hourly to 36-hourly dosing; re-audit planned in one year.
setting: Two neonatal units in one Trust
cycle1_result: 100% adhered to guideline criteria and 100% prescribed 15 mg/kg; 12 (24%) had no level at 24 hours; of 38 with 24-hour levels only 6 (16%) were <5 mg/L; 17/23 (74%) in range at 36 hours; 2 patients received doses despite levels >5 mg/L.
intervention: Recommended change from 24-hourly to 36-hourly dosing; re-audit planned in one year.
other_findings: No direct correlation seen between gestational age, severity of illness and amikacin levels.
authors: Caroline D; Tami B; Lidia T; Ioana G
citation: Caroline D, Tami B, Lidia T, Ioana G. P26 An audit of the use of amikacin for early onset sepsis in premature neonates in an inpatient neonatal unit. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e1.31-e1. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.37.

title: P34 Quality improvement project aimed at reducing gentamicin errors in neonates
standard: National Patient Safety Agency (NPSA) recommendations on gentamicin
finding: 18 gentamicin errors reported; 84% at prescribing and 16% at administration; 67% due to complexity of calculating a 36-hourly dosing interval.
change: PDSA cycles from July 2017: simplified standardised dosing interval, updated local monograph with example prescription, posters in prescribing areas, MDT feedback session, guideline promotion and error monitoring, lower-risk alternative antibiotic in low-risk babies, and gentamicin prescribing exercise at new doctor induction.
setting: Level 3 tertiary neonatal unit, 40 cots
cycle1_result: 18 gentamicin errors reported; 84% at prescribing and 16% at administration; 67% due to complexity of calculating a 36-hourly dosing interval.
intervention: PDSA cycles from July 2017: simplified standardised dosing interval, updated local monograph with example prescription, posters in prescribing areas, MDT feedback session, guideline promotion and error monitoring, lower-risk alternative antibiotic in low-risk babies, and gentamicin prescribing exercise at new doctor induction.
other_findings: Evaluation using Datix-reported errors was planned 3 months after implementation, with monthly audit to follow.
authors: Heather C; Aubrey M
citation: Heather C, Aubrey M. P34 Quality improvement project aimed at reducing gentamicin errors in neonates. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e1.38-e1. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.43.

title: P37 Audit on the quality of documentation of paediatric prescriptions using electronic prescription charts
standard: Legal prescribing requirements (Medicines Act 1968), trust Medicines Management Policy; ten standards based on RCP Generic Medical Record Keeping Standards 2017
finding: 100% compliance for most demographics and prescription items and all fluid standards; allergy status 95% (severity 93%); weight 73%; antimicrobial indication 81% and duration 46%.
change: Results presented locally and emailed to staff; recommended e-prescribing training and compulsory weight and allergy entry.
setting: Four inpatient paediatric wards using electronic prescribing
cycle1_result: 100% compliance for most demographics and prescription items and all fluid standards; allergy status 95% (severity 93%); weight 73%; antimicrobial indication 81% and duration 46%.
intervention: Results presented locally and emailed to staff; recommended e-prescribing training and compulsory weight and allergy entry.
other_findings: Electronic prescribing improved adherence compared with previous paper chart audits.
authors: Philippa S; Abimbola S
citation: Philippa S, Abimbola S. P37 Audit on the quality of documentation of paediatric prescriptions using electronic prescription charts. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e1.41-e1. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.46.

topic: Influenza vaccination and asthma prescribing in children
title: P38 An audit to assess influenza vaccination uptake amongst asthmatic children in a city in the northwest of england
standard: BTS/SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma 2016 for prescribing; influenza vaccine uptake
finding: 148 (31.2%) had flu vaccination; 194/297 (65.3%) prescriptions followed BTS guidelines.
setting: GP surgeries in Liverpool CCG (seven participating), primary care
cycle1_result: 148 (31.2%) had flu vaccination; 194/297 (65.3%) prescriptions followed BTS guidelines.
other_findings: Commonest non-compliance was salbutamol monotherapy or no medication. Low deprivation and age 5 or under associated with higher vaccination (p<0.05).
authors: Octavio A; Elisha K; Charles M; Andrew L
citation: Octavio A, Elisha K, Charles M, Andrew L. P38 An audit to assess influenza vaccination uptake amongst asthmatic children in a city in the northwest of england. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e1.42-e1. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.47.

title: P39 Continuous vancomycin dosing: an audit and evaluation
standard: Local vancomycin prescribing and therapeutic drug monitoring guidance
finding: Loading, initial continuous dosing and TDM generally in line with local guidelines; 9% of first levels subtherapeutic; of 298 levels 56% therapeutic, 19% supratherapeutic, 25% subtherapeutic
setting: Neonatal units
cycle1_result: Loading, initial continuous dosing and TDM generally in line with local guidelines; 9% of first levels subtherapeutic; of 298 levels 56% therapeutic, 19% supratherapeutic, 25% subtherapeutic
other_findings: A previous audit of intermittent dosing found 50% of first levels subtherapeutic; no vancomycin-specific adverse effects.
authors: Fiona R; Rachel W; Mildrid Y
citation: Fiona R, Rachel W, Mildrid Y. P39 Continuous vancomycin dosing: an audit and evaluation. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e1.43-e1. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.48.

topic: Uveitis screening in juvenile idiopathic arthritis
title: P41 An audit of the screening and treatment of uveitis in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (jia) at a paediatric tertiary centre
standard: BSPAR/RCO uveitis screening guidelines (screen within 6 weeks of referral); NHS England JIA treatment recommendations
finding: Referred for screening 50/54 (92.6%); screened 45/50 (90%); screened within 6 weeks of referral 8/45 (17.8%); JIA treatment in line with NHS England 100% of 41 documented.
setting: Paediatric tertiary centre and satellite clinics (Childhood Arthritis Prospective Study patients)
cycle1_result: Referred for screening 50/54 (92.6%); screened 45/50 (90%); screened within 6 weeks of referral 8/45 (17.8%); JIA treatment in line with NHS England 100% of 41 documented.
other_findings: 4/45 (8.9%) diagnosed with uveitis. Recommendations: better communication with satellite clinics and training for junior staff on screening targets.
authors: Octavio A; Amy R; Charles M
citation: Octavio A, Amy R, Charles M. P41 An audit of the screening and treatment of uveitis in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (jia) at a paediatric tertiary centre. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e1.46-e1. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.50.

title: P7 An audit of the management of resuscitation drugs and trolley contents
standard: Resuscitation Council (UK) acute care equipment and drug lists (2013) and local Trust trolley content list; daily trolley checks
finding: Drug content compliance 50%; oxygen cylinders on trolley 5/29; daily trolley checks 29/32; guidelines present on 31/32 trolleys but needed revision.
change: Trolley content list changed from 250 mL to 500 mL sodium chloride 0.9% bags kept as routine stock, and resuscitation guidelines revised for clearer paediatric dosing.
setting: 47 hospital clinical areas with resuscitation trolleys and/or emergency drug boxes
cycle1_result: Drug content compliance 50%; oxygen cylinders on trolley 5/29; daily trolley checks 29/32; guidelines present on 31/32 trolleys but needed revision.
intervention: Trolley content list changed from 250 mL to 500 mL sodium chloride 0.9% bags kept as routine stock, and resuscitation guidelines revised for clearer paediatric dosing.
other_findings: 84.4% of areas did not stock 250 mL sodium chloride bags and 20 trolleys held unlisted drugs. The resuscitation committee agreed to re-audit at least every 6 months.
authors: Maidre M; McVittie P; Isaac R
citation: Maidre M, McVittie P, Isaac R. P7 An audit of the management of resuscitation drugs and trolley contents. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e2.8-e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.16.

title: P12 An audit on the use and monitoring of azathioprine (aza) in a paediatric gastroenterology centre. could nhs england via specialist commissioning rules (nhs-e-spr) be affecting quality of care?
standard: BSPGHAN guidelines: eleven azathioprine monitoring points (clinic attendance, height, weight, baseline VZV status, TPMT, and FBC, U&Es, amylase, CRP and LFT monitoring)
finding: Only 16 patients (19%) met all eleven points; 27 (24.5%) fully compliant with blood monitoring frequency; TPMT measured in 104 (97%) but late in 48 (46%); weight and height not documented in 31 (28%) and 47 (43%); baseline VZV not checked in 23 (21%).
change: Suggested shared-care guidelines, order sets with all parameters at diagnosis and a tick-box monitoring proforma for clinic.
setting: Paediatric gastroenterology centre
cycle1_result: Only 16 patients (19%) met all eleven points; 27 (24.5%) fully compliant with blood monitoring frequency; TPMT measured in 104 (97%) but late in 48 (46%); weight and height not documented in 31 (28%) and 47 (43%); baseline VZV not checked in 23 (21%).
intervention: Suggested shared-care guidelines, order sets with all parameters at diagnosis and a tick-box monitoring proforma for clinic.
other_findings: Suboptimal monitoring correlated with living further from the centre (p=0.008) and tablet formulation (p=0.000); NHS England specialist commissioning rules prevent paediatric shared care.
authors: Jones E; Cuevas O
citation: Jones E, Cuevas O. P12 An audit on the use and monitoring of azathioprine (aza) in a paediatric gastroenterology centre. could nhs england via specialist commissioning rules (nhs-e-spr) be affecting quality of care?. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e2.14-e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.21.

title: P15 Melatonin prescribing audit
standard: Regular clinic review of melatonin treatment (efficacy, dose, duration)
finding: 238 (59%) had melatonin reviewed at follow-up; 81 (20%) attended clinic without documented review; 42 (10%) on long-term melatonin not seen for over a year; 39 (10%) newly started not followed up.
setting: Outpatient and community patients receiving melatonin from hospital pharmacy
cycle1_result: 238 (59%) had melatonin reviewed at follow-up; 81 (20%) attended clinic without documented review; 42 (10%) on long-term melatonin not seen for over a year; 39 (10%) newly started not followed up.
other_findings: Of those without review, 52 (64%) had failed to attend clinic. 26 (6.4%) were on other sedatives concurrently; re-audit planned for end of 2016.
authors: Wong S
citation: Wong S. P15 Melatonin prescribing audit. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e2.17-e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.24.

title: P16 An audit of domperidone prescribing in children
standard: MHRA May 2014 drug safety update and NPPG May 2015 statement on domperidone (dose, duration, indication, ECG monitoring in high risk, non-pharmacological trial in GORD)
finding: Dose 43/50 (86%); duration 6/50 (12%); indication 9/50 (18%); ECG monitoring in high risk 12/33 (36%); non-pharmacological trial in GORD 11/17 (64%).
change: National MHRA and NPPG alerts on domperidone.
setting: Children's hospital
cycle1_period: 1 January 2014 to before the NPPG alert (May 2015)
cycle1_result: Dose 43/50 (86%); duration 6/50 (12%); indication 9/50 (18%); ECG monitoring in high risk 12/33 (36%); non-pharmacological trial in GORD 11/17 (64%).
intervention: National MHRA and NPPG alerts on domperidone.
cycle2_result: Dose 10/10 (100%); duration 1/10 (10%); indication 1/10 (10%); ECG monitoring 0/4 (0%); non-pharmacological trial 2/3 (66%).
other_findings: Cardiac monitoring in at-risk patients remained poor; many children still received domperidone off-licence long term.
authors: Williams L; Olalekan K; Cole C; Fox A
citation: Williams L, Olalekan K, Cole C, Fox A. P16 An audit of domperidone prescribing in children. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2018;103(2):e2.18-e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.25.

topic: Enoxaparin prescribing and anti-Xa monitoring in children
title: P17 An audit of enoxaparin prescribing and monitoring in child health
standard: BNFc dosing and anti-Xa monitoring
finding: 71% (n=17) of therapeutic prescriptions dosed per BNFc; 35% had anti-Xa within 36 hours; 71% of levels taken 4–6 hours post dose; 82% (n=11) out-of-range levels led to dose change, 56% (n=9) rechecked within 24 hours; 76% (n=25) prophylactic prescriptions per BNFc.
setting: Children's Hospital
cycle1_result: 71% (n=17) of therapeutic prescriptions dosed per BNFc; 35% had anti-Xa within 36 hours; 71% of levels taken 4–6 hours post dose; 82% (n=11) out-of-range levels led to dose change, 56% (n=9) rechecked within 24 hours; 76% (n=25) prophylactic prescriptions per BNFc.

authors: Main C; Hibberd S; Cole C

title: P39 Start smart: improving the quality of empiric antimicrobial prescribing at a tertiary paediatric hospital
standard: Local antimicrobial guidelines: ≥90% of children admitted via ED and started on antibiotics have a documented indication and guideline-compliant choice
finding: Documentation of indication and guideline compliance median 30%.
change: Weekly audit feedback with run charts, antibiotic discussion at Monday handover, prescriber spot quiz, updated guidelines and prescribing app, ID badge guideline cards, and reminders at point of prescribing in ED.
setting: Emergency department admissions, tertiary paediatric hospital
cycle1_result: Documentation of indication and guideline compliance median 30%.
intervention: Weekly audit feedback with run charts, antibiotic discussion at Monday handover, prescriber spot quiz, updated guidelines and prescribing app, ID badge guideline cards, and reminders at point of prescribing in ED.
cycle2_result: Documentation of indication and guideline compliance 100% consistently.
other_findings: Weekly audits sampled the first ten children admitted via ED on antibiotics; improvement persisted through three NCHD changeovers. Antimicrobial expenditure fell by €101,078.44 from 2014 to 2015.
authors: Kirrane M; Cunney R; McNamara R; Okafor I

topic: Home breast milk fortifier after preterm discharge
title: Home use of breast milk fortifier to promote postdischarge growth and breast feeding in preterm infants: a quality improvement project.
standard: Use of breast milk fortifier after discharge until 48 weeks' gestational age
finding: not reported
change: Electronic patient information sheet promoting home breast milk fortifier, developed over four PDSA cycles.
setting: Tertiary surgical neonatal unit, University Hospital Southampton
cycle1_result: not reported
intervention: Electronic patient information sheet promoting home breast milk fortifier, developed over four PDSA cycles.

title: P003 Intermittent vancomycin in paediatrics: implementation and audit of a new guideline
standard: Trust intermittent IV vancomycin guideline (2016) with loading dose and increased dose and frequency versus BNFC
finding: Pre-implementation audit: 7% of levels in therapeutic range at 48 hours; lack of support for appropriate dosing and monitoring.
change: New trust guideline for intermittent IV vancomycin (loading dose, higher dose and frequency) with pharmacist intervention.
setting: Paediatric wards (patients ≥1 month) on intermittent IV vancomycin
cycle1_result: Pre-implementation audit: 7% of levels in therapeutic range at 48 hours; lack of support for appropriate dosing and monitoring.
intervention: New trust guideline for intermittent IV vancomycin (loading dose, higher dose and frequency) with pharmacist intervention.
cycle2_result: Loading dose used appropriately in 83%; levels at correct times in 90%; 40% in range at 48 hours; 100% reviewed at 48 hours; out-of-range levels reviewed per guideline in 40%, rising to 80% with pharmacist intervention.

title: P014 An audit assessing the prescribing of naloxone in paediatric patients
standard: Local Multidisciplinary Guidelines for Acute Pain Management in Children and Young People: all patients on opioids have PRN naloxone with correct directions
finding: Naloxone prescribed in 17% (7/41); on PRN section 100% (7/7); correct directions 86% (6/7).
change: Planned: presentation at paediatric and surgical paediatric audit meetings to educate prescribers.
setting: Paediatric inpatient wards
cycle1_result: Naloxone prescribed in 17% (7/41); on PRN section 100% (7/7); correct directions 86% (6/7).
intervention: Planned: presentation at paediatric and surgical paediatric audit meetings to educate prescribers.
other_findings: not reported
authors: Ntanganika E; Patel B

topic: Vitamin D supplementation in children and pregnancy
title: P020 Vitamin supplementation survey: an audit of the usage of vitamin D supplementation in paediatric patients, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers
standard: SACN (2016) vitamin D recommendations and local guidelines
finding: Under 30% of parents (16/54) received advice on childhood vitamin supplementation; 24.5% of children (25/102) received supplementation. 77% (30/39) of pregnant/breastfeeding mothers received advice but only 54% (21) took supplements.
setting: Two hospitals, pharmacist-led data collection
cycle1_result: Under 30% of parents (16/54) received advice on childhood vitamin supplementation; 24.5% of children (25/102) received supplementation. 77% (30/39) of pregnant/breastfeeding mothers received advice but only 54% (21) took supplements.
other_findings: 93 of 164 questionnaires returned (57%). Midwives and health visitors most often gave advice.
authors: Thomas L; Patel B
citation: Thomas L, Patel B. P020 Vitamin supplementation survey: an audit of the usage of vitamin D supplementation in paediatric patients, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2019;104(7):e2.24-e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2019-nppc.30.

title: P029 Audit of aciclovir prescribing to assess whether changing the order of drop down box options in an electronic prescribing system can reduce prescribing errors
standard: Aciclovir dosing per BNF for Children and trust empirical antibiotic guidelines
finding: 26% (9/35) of aciclovir doses incorrect; wrong drop-down option chosen in 78% (7/9) of incorrect prescriptions.
change: Aciclovir drop-down options in the electronic prescribing system reordered so the most frequently used option appeared first (from 01/02/17).
setting: Paediatric intensive care unit
cycle1_result: 26% (9/35) of aciclovir doses incorrect; wrong drop-down option chosen in 78% (7/9) of incorrect prescriptions.
intervention: Aciclovir drop-down options in the electronic prescribing system reordered so the most frequently used option appeared first (from 01/02/17).
cycle2_result: 17% (5/30) of doses incorrect; wrong drop-down option in 0% (0/5) of incorrect prescriptions.
other_findings: Error rate was 14% (7/50) when the correct drop-down was chosen vs 47% (7/15) when the wrong option was selected.
authors: Gunning C; Gray J
citation: Gunning C, Gray J. P029 Audit of aciclovir prescribing to assess whether changing the order of drop down box options in an electronic prescribing system can reduce prescribing errors. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2019;104(7):e2.33-e2. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2019-nppc.39.

title: Prediagnosis pathway benchmarking audit in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
standard: Benchmark criteria from a prior single-centre UK audit of the DMD prediagnosis pathway

finding: 76.4% of patients had ALL done; 67.2% of completions green, 15.5% amber, 17.2% red; QRISK 70%, alcohol 58%, diet 82%, exercise 70%, diabetes 58%, smoking 76%.
setting: Pine Ward, 17-bed male low secure forensic inpatient ward, Sussex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust
cycle1_result: 76.4% of patients had ALL done; 67.2% of completions green, 15.5% amber, 17.2% red; QRISK 70%, alcohol 58%, diet 82%, exercise 70%, diabetes 58%, smoking 76%.

standard: NICE NG97 (June 2018) Dementia guideline and local trust guidance on antipsychotic prescribing and monitoring.
finding: 88% had assessment of sources of distress; 42% had non-pharmacological intervention before antipsychotic (58% after starting); 63% risk discussion documented; 63% baseline bloods; 54% baseline ECG; 33% of those treated over 12 weeks had discontinuation or dose-reduction trial; under 22% had physical health monitoring at one year.
setting: Harrogate Older Adult Community Mental Health Team, Tees Esk and Wear Valleys NHS Foundation Trust
cycle1_result: 88% had assessment of sources of distress; 42% had non-pharmacological intervention before antipsychotic (58% after starting); 63% risk discussion documented; 63% baseline bloods; 54% baseline ECG; 33% of those treated over 12 weeks had discontinuation or dose-reduction trial; under 22% had physical health monitoring at one year.
other_findings: Random sample of 24 from 55 patients. Recommended a pre-prescribing checklist and a system to flag when monitoring and review are due.
authors: Wilson J; White N; Croft M; Ahmed S; Illsley L; Hughes P

topic: Psychosocial intervention uptake in dementia memory services
title: An Audit on the Uptake of Psychosocial Interventions in a Nationally Accredited Memory Service
standard: NICE guideline NG97 'Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers'; Memory Services National Accreditation Programme (MSNAP) Standards
finding: 23/140 (16.4%) patients referred to the Recovery College by a single referrer (12 booked workshops, 4 declined); only 11.4% (16/140) of clinic letters documented referral and none stated a rationale; compliance was 100% for trained staff delivering workshops, access to interventions for challenging behaviour, and assessment/interventions for carers' needs; 99.3% (139/140) were offered pharmacological intervention or had the exception documented.
setting: Jocelyn Solly Resource Centre, nationally accredited memory service
cycle1_result: 23/140 (16.4%) patients referred to the Recovery College by a single referrer (12 booked workshops, 4 declined); only 11.4% (16/140) of clinic letters documented referral and none stated a rationale; compliance was 100% for trained staff delivering workshops, access to interventions for challenging behaviour, and assessment/interventions for carers' needs; 99.3% (139/140) were offered pharmacological intervention or had the exception documented.
other_findings: No access to individual/maintenance Cognitive Stimulation Therapy, art/creative therapies or psychology/occupational therapy input due to staff vacancies; recommendations include amending clinic letter proformas, staff education and multidisciplinary review of Recovery College referrals.
authors: Winfield S; Zafar F; Williamson T; Cooper-Hunt M
citation: Winfield S, Zafar F, Williamson T, Cooper-Hunt M. An Audit on the Uptake of Psychosocial Interventions in a Nationally Accredited Memory Service. BJPsych Open. 2023;9(Suppl 1):S188-S188.

title: Improving Acute Treatment of Alcohol Withdrawal at an Inpatient De-addiction Ward (‘Vimukthi’) at Kerala State, India: Full Cycle of a Clinical Audit
standard: ASAM, NICE and Government of India guidelines: long-acting benzodiazepines with fixed-dose, symptom-triggered or front-loading regimens according to setting and risk
finding: Fixed-dose regimen of short-acting lorazepam used for all patients; no documentation of risk profiling.
change: Standard operating procedure with risk profiling, symptom-triggered regimen using nurse-administered CIWA-Ar and front-loading for high risk, introduced after team discussion and training in October 2023.
setting: Dedicated 10-bed inpatient de-addiction ward ('Vimukthi') attached to a general hospital, Kerala
cycle1_result: Fixed-dose regimen of short-acting lorazepam used for all patients; no documentation of risk profiling.
intervention: Standard operating procedure with risk profiling, symptom-triggered regimen using nurse-administered CIWA-Ar and front-loading for high risk, introduced after team discussion and training in October 2023.
cycle2_result: Risk stratification documented (34% low, 52% intermediate, 14% high risk); symptom-triggered regimen given to all patients with front-loading for all high-risk patients; oral lorazepam fell from 3324 mg for 63 patients (Oct–Dec 2022) to 10 mg for 39 patients.
other_findings: Injectable lorazepam use rose by 25% (0.8 mg to 1 mg per patient) and oral diazepam rose from nil to 170 mg. Staff and patients reported satisfaction with the new protocol.
authors: S A; Kuriakose A; Sathiaseelan R
citation: S A, Kuriakose A, Sathiaseelan R. Improving Acute Treatment of Alcohol Withdrawal at an Inpatient De-addiction Ward (‘Vimukthi’) at Kerala State, India: Full Cycle of a Clinical Audit. BJPsych Open. 2024;10(S1):S14-S15. doi:10.1192/bjo.2024.100.

title: Improving the Quality of Junior Doctor Handover in Tyrone and Fermanagh Hospital, Northern Ireland
standard: not reported
finding: Password protection used in 69%; other baseline figures not reported.

finding: 4/14 formally diagnosed with BPSD; 6/14 on antipsychotics, of which 1/6 fully met NICE standards; 2/14 had structured assessment tools used
change: PDSA cycles with a ward-round checklist and staff education

intervention: PDSA cycles with a ward-round checklist and staff education

other_findings: Small numbers; further PDSA cycles suggested for sustainability.

topic: Physical health information in psychiatric discharge summaries

standard: Criteria and standards for physical health review information in discharge summaries, derived from a team questionnaire

change: Proposed solution to be implemented (not described)

cycle1_result: Only 49% of service users with physical health reviews had any information provided on discharge; content varied and was inconsistent
intervention: Proposed solution to be implemented (not described)

topic: Mental Health Act consent to treatment documentation
title: Improving Capacity and Consent to Treatment Recording, Park House Hospital
standard: Trust Consent to Treatment policy
finding: not reported
change: Interactive consent to treatment teaching for core trainees, presentation to the Trust MHA/MCA quality improvement group, and consultation with pharmacists and consultants on ward recording systems
setting: All inpatient wards, Park House Hospital, Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
cycle1_result: not reported
intervention: Interactive consent to treatment teaching for core trainees, presentation to the Trust MHA/MCA quality improvement group, and consultation with pharmacists and consultants on ward recording systems
cycle2_result: No ward had 100% capacity forms documented, kept in charts and uploaded; 7/9 wards 100% for completing T2/T3/S62 forms; 6/9 wards 100% for retaining them in charts; 78% uploaded to PARIS; 80% of medication charts matched T2/T3 forms
other_findings: Only 24% of trainees felt confident about consent to treatment and 32% checked forms before prescribing; 91% said teaching helped. Ward round proformas and monthly ward auditing were proposed.
authors: McKnight R; Fu R

title: Assessing the Anticholinergic Burden in the West Memory Assessment Service (MAS)
standard: Anticholinergic burden (ACB) score documented for patients referred to the memory assessment service
finding: No documented ACB scores at referral; calculated scores varied by tool, with the lowest suggesting 20.4% (n = 10) had a raised ACB score
change: Planned: standardised ACB tool for all new referrals and improved awareness across the memory pathway

cycle1_result: No documented ACB scores at referral; calculated scores varied by tool, with the lowest suggesting 20.4% (n = 10) had a raised ACB score
intervention: Planned: standardised ACB tool for all new referrals and improved awareness across the memory pathway
other_findings: Amitriptyline was the commonest contributor to anticholinergic burden in all three scoring systems. Re-audit planned in 3 months.
authors: Lees R; Alderson J
citation: Lees R, Alderson J. Assessing the Anticholinergic Burden in the West Memory Assessment Service (MAS). BJPsych Open. 2022;8(Suppl 1):S163-S163.

topic: COVID-19 vaccination in mental health patients
title: Improving COVID-19 Vaccination Uptake in Service Users Admitted to an Acute Inpatient Psychiatric Ward
standard: Aim that every newly admitted unvaccinated patient has vaccination status documented and is offered the appropriate COVID-19 vaccine dose

title: Physical Health Monitoring of Patients Prescribed Depot Antipsychotic Medication in North West Edinburgh Community Mental Health Team (CMHT)
standard: SIGN guidelines: annual physical health monitoring for all patients on antipsychotic medication (9 domains)
finding: Domains achieved in 8% (lipid monitoring) to 51% (glucose monitoring)
change: Physical health questionnaire and staff training in phlebotomy and ECG, followed by a dedicated physical health monitoring clinic
setting: North West Edinburgh Community Mental Health Team, NHS Lothian
cycle1_result: Domains achieved in 8% (lipid monitoring) to 51% (glucose monitoring)
intervention: Physical health questionnaire and staff training in phlebotomy and ECG, followed by a dedicated physical health monitoring clinic
cycle2_result: Decline in all domains from 2020, but 66% of domains still improved compared with 2019
other_findings: At the 2020 re-audit (74 patients) 77% of domains had improved, including blood pressure 9% to 37%, ECG 20% to 43% and lipids 29% to 46%; the later decline was attributed to COVID-19.
authors: Klejnotowska A; Bailey R; Thompson A; Wojtowicz J; Haggart J; Evans H; Choi H; Mallis A; MacLeod A; Murdie D; Argent V
citation: Klejnotowska A, Bailey R, Thompson A, Wojtowicz J, Haggart J, Evans H, et al.. Physical Health Monitoring of Patients Prescribed Depot Antipsychotic Medication in North West Edinburgh Community Mental Health Team (CMHT). BJPsych Open. 2022;8(Suppl 1):S149-S150.

title: Monitoring of Patients Who Presented With First Episode Psychosis, Under the Early Intervention Team, Against NICE Guidance for Psychosis and Schizophrenia
standard: NICE psychosis and schizophrenia guidance: physical health monitoring at defined intervals after starting antipsychotics (e.g. BP at 12 weeks and 1 year)
finding: Overall compliance 51%; weight/BMI and waist circumference 0%; pulse and BP 43% (90% by 1 year); lipids 48% (86% within a year); prolactin 52%; FBC 86%, U&E 86%, LFT 90%; glucose/HbA1c 48%; ECG at 1 year 67%
change: Recommended: disseminate results through the team, add waist circumference to the physical health assessment form and create blood sample sets
setting: Early Intervention Team, Warrington and Halton
cycle1_result: Overall compliance 51%; weight/BMI and waist circumference 0%; pulse and BP 43% (90% by 1 year); lipids 48% (86% within a year); prolactin 52%; FBC 86%, U&E 86%, LFT 90%; glucose/HbA1c 48%; ECG at 1 year 67%
intervention: Recommended: disseminate results through the team, add waist circumference to the physical health assessment form and create blood sample sets
other_findings: COVID-19 limiting in-person appointments, staff redeployment and disengagement may have lowered compliance. Re-audit planned.
authors: Khanna R
citation: Khanna R. Monitoring of Patients Who Presented With First Episode Psychosis, Under the Early Intervention Team, Against NICE Guidance for Psychosis and Schizophrenia. BJPsych Open. 2022;8(Suppl 1):S161-S161.

title: Prescribing and Monitoring of High Dose Antipsychotic Therapy (HDAT) in the Acute Inpatient Setting
standard: Royal College of Psychiatrists HDAT guidance: documented rationale, risk-benefit discussion or capacity/legal process, and ECG, BMI and blood monitoring
finding: 3/49 (6%) on HDAT, with no documented rationale and variable physical health monitoring
change: Education sessions for rotational junior doctors in the six months after the initial audit
setting: Three acute general adult inpatient wards, Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
cycle1_result: 3/49 (6%) on HDAT, with no documented rationale and variable physical health monitoring
intervention: Education sessions for rotational junior doctors in the six months after the initial audit
cycle2_result: 11/47 (23%) on HDAT; only 2 of 7 MDT/consultant-initiated cases noted HDAT initiation; 8 had ECG within a month before HDAT; only 3 had repeat ECG within 7 days

standard: Post-ligature assessment including ABCDE documentation, NEWS monitoring and follow-up plan
finding: Medic informed in 4; 0 ABCDE documentation; 0 NEWS monitoring; 3 follow-up plans.
change: Locality teaching on audit findings, post-ligature assessment tool, and trial in simulation induction for new trainees.
setting: Langley Green Hospital, Sussex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust
cycle1_result: Medic informed in 4; 0 ABCDE documentation; 0 NEWS monitoring; 3 follow-up plans.
intervention: Locality teaching on audit findings, post-ligature assessment tool, and trial in simulation induction for new trainees.
cycle2_result: Medic informed in 4; 0 ABCDE documentation; NEWS monitored in 6; 4 follow-up plans.

title: Buckinghamshire Early Intervention Service’ (BEIS) Compliance With the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines: Practical Challenges, Including Those Posed by the Pandemic, in an Outpatient Setting
standard: NICE antipsychotic monitoring guidelines (updated September 2021); 80% compliance target per National Clinical Audit of Psychosis
finding: First three months after initiation: 6/9 parameters met standard (range 2% to 100%), failing weekly BMI, pulse, BP and one-month HbA1c; only 2 parameters met for outpatient initiations; after three months only 3/9 met (lipids, HbA1c, side effects)
change: Planned: checklist for medical and nursing staff and home monitoring of blood pressure and weight by patients
setting: Buckinghamshire Early Intervention Service, Oxford Health, outpatient
cycle1_result: First three months after initiation: 6/9 parameters met standard (range 2% to 100%), failing weekly BMI, pulse, BP and one-month HbA1c; only 2 parameters met for outpatient initiations; after three months only 3/9 met (lipids, HbA1c, side effects)
intervention: Planned: checklist for medical and nursing staff and home monitoring of blood pressure and weight by patients
other_findings: Barriers included reduced contact during the pandemic, poor awareness, poor documentation of declined screening and impractical guidance such as weekly BMI. Re-audit in 6 months.
authors: Tan S; Butt H; Pike G; Williams B; Breton A; Reid A
citation: Tan S, Butt H, Pike G, Williams B, Breton A, Reid A. Buckinghamshire Early Intervention Service’ (BEIS) Compliance With the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines: Practical Challenges, Including Those Posed by the Pandemic, in an Outpatient Setting. cycle1_result: 11 plans completed with 2 more required but missing; non-pharmacological de-escalation 2/11; regular medication 5/11; rapid tranquillisation advice 8/11; absconsion risk 8/11; observation level 10/11

title: N20 Safety of extended blood monitoring for adult Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) patients on oral azathioprine during the COVID-19 pandemic: a single-centre audit
standard: Locally agreed standards for extended 6-monthly blood monitoring during COVID-19 (ECCO advises 3-monthly)
finding: 54% (n = 50) had extended blood monitoring, of whom 43 (86%) were eligible; one had raised ALT that improved after a treatment break; one advice-line call for side effects; no admissions due to deranged bloods or adverse effects
setting: IBD service, St Mark's Hospital, London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust
cycle1_result: 54% (n = 50) had extended blood monitoring, of whom 43 (86%) were eligible; one had raised ALT that improved after a treatment break; one advice-line call for side effects; no admissions due to deranged bloods or adverse effects

authors: Al-Hasani A; Younge L; Chana A

title: 48 Consenting Surgical Patients for the Risk Associated with Contracting COVID-19 During Their Stay at the Hospital
standard: Royal College of Surgeons guidance on consent during COVID-19, Section 3A (discuss risk of contracting COVID-19 in hospital)
finding: 37% consented for risk of contracting COVID-19
change: Teaching sessions, regular emails to the general surgical department and posters in common areas, repeated each cycle
setting: General surgical department, large NHS Trust in London (BHRUT)
cycle1_result: 37% consented for risk of contracting COVID-19
intervention: Teaching sessions, regular emails to the general surgical department and posters in common areas, repeated each cycle
cycle2_result: 85% consented for COVID-19 risk (fourth cycle); significant increase from first cycle
other_findings: Four cycles in total (n = 38, 41, 28, 32; 139 patients) with compliance 37%, 61%, 71% and 85%.

citation: Al Aaraj M, Abdeen B, Alkilani Y, Kaul S, Yang Y, Wain M. 48 Consenting Surgical Patients for the Risk Associated with Contracting COVID-19 During Their Stay at the Hospital. Br J Surg. 2022;109(Suppl 1).

title: An audit of acute respiratory antibiotic prescribing in COPD patients during the COVID-19 pandemic
standard: NICE NG114, NG168 and local formulary: 100% no prophylactic antibiotics for COVID-19; 100% no antibiotics for COVID-19 symptoms; 90% of regimens adherent to guidelines
finding: Standard 1 100% adherence; standard 2 99.4% (2 patients given antibiotics for suspected COVID-19); standard 3 only 28.7% adherent, mainly due to 7-day rather than 5-day courses.
setting: 12 general practices in a primary care network (North Solihull)
cycle1_result: Standard 1 100% adherence; standard 2 99.4% (2 patients given antibiotics for suspected COVID-19); standard 3 only 28.7% adherent, mainly due to 7-day rather than 5-day courses.
other_findings: Antibiotic prescribing did not change significantly between 2019 and 2020 (1029 vs 1134 prescriptions; p>0.05). Re-audit suggested after NG191.
authors: Thompson J; Widdows G; Parbat M
journal: The International journal of pharmacy practice
citation: Thompson J, Widdows G, Parbat M. An audit of acute respiratory antibiotic prescribing in COPD patients during the COVID-19 pandemic. Int J Pharm Pract. 2022;30(Suppl 1):i24-i24.

title: WE6.2 The true cost of pre-operative investigations
standard: National guidance on preoperative investigations by ASA grade and type of surgery
finding: Only 99 of 216 blood tests required; 54% unnecessary (£690.77 over 2 months).
change: Universal guidance poster and teaching sessions
setting: Breast unit pre-operative assessment
cycle1_result: Only 99 of 216 blood tests required; 54% unnecessary (£690.77 over 2 months).
intervention: Universal guidance poster and teaching sessions
cycle2_result: 57 fewer tests and 40 fewer incorrect tests; saving of £183.46 (£1110.76 per year).
other_findings: not reported
citation: . WE6.2 The true cost of pre-operative investigations. Br J Surg. 2022;109(Suppl 5).

title: TH2.8 Continuing fast-track (Expedited) pancreaticoduodenectomy service during the Covid-19 pandemic: Experience from an established pancreatic surgical centre
standard: NICE NG85: avoid preoperative biliary drainage to allow early curative surgery
finding: not reported
change: Additional theatre sessions obtained and a fast-track referral pathway established after the prior audit.
setting: Tertiary pancreatic (HPB) surgery centre
cycle1_result: not reported
intervention: Additional theatre sessions obtained and a fast-track referral pathway established after the prior audit.
cycle2_result: 42/71 received preoperative biliary drainage; 29 did not. Median imaging to surgery 21 days (3–42) without drainage vs 62 days (22–305) with drainage (p=0.00028).
other_findings: No significant difference in HDU/ITU stay, Clavien-Dindo >2 complications (30% vs 27.8%), R0 rates or hospital stay. COVID-19 constraints likely increased drainage rates.
citation: . TH2.8 Continuing fast-track (Expedited) pancreaticoduodenectomy service during the Covid-19 pandemic: Experience from an established pancreatic surgical centre. Br J Surg. 2022;109(Suppl 5).

title: TU3.4 A relook into the effects of Covid-19 on emergency theatre utilisation
standard: not reported
finding: Baseline sending, anaesthetic, operating and recovery times (values not reported).
change: Established COVID-19 testing protocols and recommendations from first audit, including a second emergency theatre.
setting: Emergency theatres, district general hospital
cycle1_result: Baseline sending, anaesthetic, operating and recovery times (values not reported).
intervention: Established COVID-19 testing protocols and recommendations from first audit, including a second emergency theatre.
cycle2_result: Sending time decreased by 27% (p=1.25*10–7); anaesthetic time decreased by 31% (p=0.0001); recovery time in theatre decreased by 26% (p = 0.06); total recovery time increased by 19% (p=0.097).
other_findings: Sending time also 17% better than pre-pandemic figures.
citation: . TU3.4 A relook into the effects of Covid-19 on emergency theatre utilisation. Br J Surg. 2022;109(Suppl 5).

title: 541 Pre-Operative Assessment of Patients Undergoing Elective TURBT or Rigid Cystoscopy + Bladder Biopsy: Is a Group & Save Clinically Required?
standard: not reported

cycle1_result: 32.8% (21/64) had a preoperative group and save; 98.4% (63/64) had Hb measured; no transfusions required.

title: Lithium monitoring in clinical practice

topic: Vaccination uptake in immunosuppressed rheumatology patients

topic: Developmentally supportive positioning of preterm infants

title: Outcome of audit and education on blood transfusion practice in obstetrics setting.
standard: RCOG blood transfusion in obstetrics guidance (Green-top Guideline no. 47)
finding: 214 transfusion episodes in 51 patients; FFP was the most misused component, then whole blood; whole blood 34.5%, single unit transfusion 23.3%.

cycle1_result: 214 transfusion episodes in 51 patients; FFP was the most misused component, then whole blood; whole blood 34.5%, single unit transfusion 23.3%.

title: Community-Based Interventions to Reduce Child Stunting in Rural Guatemala: A Quality Improvement Model.

title: Simple steps to prevent hospital-acquired pneumonia in non-intubated patients: a quality improvement project.

finding: Three audit cycles over 6 months totalling 222 inpatients; baseline figures not reported in abstract.
change: Interventions between cycles promoting raising bedheads to 30 degrees, sitting patients out of bed for meals, discouraging straws and regular mouth care

cycle1_result: Three audit cycles over 6 months totalling 222 inpatients; baseline figures not reported in abstract.

authors: Wilkinson A; Singal A; Ramadan G
journal: British journal of nursing (Mark Allen Publishing)

finding: Majority of hospitals did not meet all EASL standards; lowest achievement for optimal UDCA dosing, bone density assessment and symptom assessment
setting: 11 NHS hospitals in England, Wales and Scotland (national pilot audit)
cycle1_result: Majority of hospitals did not meet all EASL standards; lowest achievement for optimal UDCA dosing, bone density assessment and symptom assessment
other_findings: Significant variation between trusts in these standards and in assessment of biochemical response to UDCA. PBC Review tool developed for future re-audit.

title: Analysis of neurosurgical procedures with unplanned reoperation for quality improvement: A 5-year single hospital study.
standard: Unplanned return to the operating room within 30 days as a quality metric
finding: 93 (2%) unplanned returns within 30 days; haemorrhage 49.5% (46/93) of cranial returns; median interval 3 days (IQR 1-9)

cycle1_result: 93 (2%) unplanned returns within 30 days; haemorrhage 49.5% (46/93) of cranial returns; median interval 3 days (IQR 1-9)

title: Response to winter pressures in acute services: analysis from the Winter Society for Acute Medicine Benchmarking Audit.
standard: Survey questions derived from national guidance
finding: All services had taken measures for increased demand; 81.7% had expanded medical inpatient beds and 80.4% had added extra clinical staff.

cycle1_result: All services had taken measures for increased demand; 81.7% had expanded medical inpatient beds and 80.4% had added extra clinical staff.
