topic: Peritoneal dialysis catheter removal at transplant
title: Outcomes of removal of peritoneal dialysis catheter at the time of renal transplant.
standard: not reported
finding: Mean time to PD catheter removal after transplant 84 days; 4 (10%) exit-site infection
change: Practice changed to remove all PD catheters at the time of transplant
setting: Nottingham Renal and Kidney Transplant Unit, City Hospital
cycle1_result: Mean time to PD catheter removal after transplant 84 days; 4 (10%) exit-site infection
intervention: Practice changed to remove all PD catheters at the time of transplant
cycle2_result: 19 of 20 had PD catheter removed at transplant; one required re-insertion
other_findings: The one patient with catheter left in situ developed peritonitis.
authors: Parks RM; Saedon M
journal: Saudi journal of kidney diseases and transplantation : an official publication of the Saudi Center for Organ Transplantation, Saudi Arabia
citation: Parks RM, Saedon M. Outcomes of removal of peritoneal dialysis catheter at the time of renal transplant. Saudi J Kidney Dis Transpl. 2021;32(2):415-417. doi:10.4103/1319-2442.335453. PMID: 35017335.

topic: Secondary prevention after acute coronary syndrome
title: Implementation of clinical audit to improve adherence to guideline-recommended therapy in acute coronary syndrome.
standard: Guideline-directed medical therapy at discharge (statins, dual antiplatelet therapy, beta-blockers, ACE-I/ARB) with no unjustifiable omissions
finding: Unreasonable omissions in first month: DAPT 1%, statin 0%, ACE-I/ARB 14%, beta-blockers 11%.
change: Clinical pharmacist-led monthly audit with feedback report presented to cardiologists.
setting: Department of Cardiology, PSG Institute of Medical Sciences and Research, Coimbatore
cycle1_result: Unreasonable omissions in first month: DAPT 1%, statin 0%, ACE-I/ARB 14%, beta-blockers 11%.
intervention: Clinical pharmacist-led monthly audit with feedback report presented to cardiologists.
cycle2_result: Unreasonable omissions reduced to nil by the end of the 11th month and stayed nil to the 12th month.
other_findings: 1072 is the total audited over 12 months; improvement sustained to month 12.
authors: George NE; Shukkoor AA; Joseph N; Palanimuthu R; Kaliappan T; Gopalan R
journal: The Egyptian heart journal : (EHJ) : official bulletin of the Egyptian Society of Cardiology
citation: George NE, Shukkoor AA, Joseph N, Palanimuthu R, Kaliappan T, Gopalan R. Implementation of clinical audit to improve adherence to guideline-recommended therapy in acute coronary syndrome. Egypt Heart J. 2022;74(1):4. doi:10.1186/s43044-021-00237-7. PMID: 35020077.

title: An audit of dental assessments including orthopantomography and timing of dental extractions before radiotherapy for head and neck cancer.
standard: National guidelines for pre-radiotherapy dental assessment including OPG and extraction timing
finding: 89% (129) had an OPG and 72% (104) had a pre-radiotherapy dental assessment; 47 had extractions a median 13 days before radiotherapy.
setting: Regional Oncology Centre, Liverpool University Hospitals; consecutive cohort from MDT records
cycle1_period: January to March 2018 and January to March 2019
cycle1_result: 89% (129) had an OPG and 72% (104) had a pre-radiotherapy dental assessment; 47 had extractions a median 13 days before radiotherapy.
other_findings: Oral and laryngeal sites had the most missed assessments; no osteoradionecrosis by November 2020.
authors: King R; Li C; Lowe D; Rogers SN
citation: King R, Li C, Lowe D, Rogers SN. An audit of dental assessments including orthopantomography and timing of dental extractions before radiotherapy for head and neck cancer. Br Dent J. 2022;232(1):38-43. doi:10.1038/s41415-021-3823-0. PMID: 35031745.

title: Better opioid prescribing in an inpatient oncology unit: quality improvement project.
standard: Safe prescribing and best practice opioid prescribing standards
finding: 76% met safe prescribing and 68% best practice.
change: Quality improvement project from September 2020 with several interventions including opioid prescribing guidelines
setting: Inpatient oncology unit, tertiary cancer centre (St Bartholomew's Hospital), London
cycle1_result: 76% met safe prescribing and 68% best practice.
intervention: Quality improvement project from September 2020 with several interventions including opioid prescribing guidelines
cycle2_result: 87% met safe prescribing and 56% best practice.
other_findings: Second audit in February 2020 after an opioid education programme showed deterioration: 61% safe prescribing and 39% best practice.
authors: Weil A; Vijeratnam SS; Potter V; Teli J; Feuer D
citation: Weil A, Vijeratnam SS, Potter V, Teli J, Feuer D. Better opioid prescribing in an inpatient oncology unit: quality improvement project. BMJ Support Palliat Care. 2024;13(e3):e1379-e1382. doi:10.1136/bmjspcare-2021-003477. PMID: 35045978.

title: Is it True Hypoparathyroidism? A Root Cause Analysis of Unusually Low Intact Parathyroid Hormone (iPTH) at a Clinical Laboratory.
standard: Pre-analytical steps for intact PTH samples (prompt separation, cold chain)
finding: 110 (4.3%) apparently falsely low; 60 (2.4%) normal or raised on recollection.
change: Online meetings with staff country-wide and flyers on pre-analytical steps by email and hard copy
setting: Section of Clinical Chemistry, Aga Khan University Hospital, Karachi
cycle1_result: 110 (4.3%) apparently falsely low; 60 (2.4%) normal or raised on recollection.
intervention: Online meetings with staff country-wide and flyers on pre-analytical steps by email and hard copy
cycle2_result: 30 apparently falsely low; 14 (0.96%) confirmed falsely low.
other_findings: Causes were delayed sample separation and poor temperature chain maintenance.
authors: Ahmed S; Jafri L; Shah SMA; Bano N; Siddiqui I
citation: Ahmed S, Jafri L, Shah SMA, Bano N, Siddiqui I. Is it True Hypoparathyroidism? A Root Cause Analysis of Unusually Low Intact Parathyroid Hormone (iPTH) at a Clinical Laboratory. EJIFCC. 2021;32(4):442-450. PMID: 35046762.

topic: Transgender patient care in primary care
title: Care of Transgender Patients: A General Practice Quality Improvement Approach.
standard: International secondary care evidence-informed guideline (no primary care standard found)
finding: Up to two-thirds of patients did not receive all recommended monitoring standards.
setting: One primary care population, Falmouth and Penryn Primary Care Network, Cornwall
cycle1_result: Up to two-thirds of patients did not receive all recommended monitoring standards.
other_findings: Long waits and high medical complexity were found; a fifth of patients stopped hormones, more than half of whom cited regret or detransition.
authors: Boyd I; Hackett T; Bewley S
citation: Boyd I, Hackett T, Bewley S. Care of Transgender Patients: A General Practice Quality Improvement Approach. Healthcare (Basel). 2022;10(1):121. doi:10.3390/healthcare10010121. PMID: 35052285.

title: Postcode Lottery in Healthcare? Findings from the Scottish National Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment in Secondary Care Audit 2019.
standard: not reported
finding: 26 of 28 hospitals responded (92.9%); significant variation in frailty units, admission routes, staffing, liaison and rehabilitation.
setting: Scottish hospitals receiving acute admissions
cycle1_result: 26 of 28 hospitals responded (92.9%); significant variation in frailty units, admission routes, staffing, liaison and rehabilitation.
other_findings: Service-level questionnaire audit.
authors: Young C; Donaldson AIC; McAlpine CH; Locherty M; Wood AD; Myint PK

topic: Night-time noise and light in critical care
title: Improving critical care patients' sleep quality in a surgical high-dependency unit: An evidence-based practice project.
standard: JBI-based audit of nurses' adherence to sleep promotion activities, threshold 80%
finding: Sleep quality (Richards-Campbell) mean 53 (SD 19.89); adherence figures not reported.
change: Evidence-based sleep promotion practice, including grouping nursing activities and reducing light and noise at night.
setting: 24-bed surgical high-dependency unit, public tertiary hospital (National University Hospital)
cycle1_result: Sleep quality (Richards-Campbell) mean 53 (SD 19.89); adherence figures not reported.
intervention: Evidence-based sleep promotion practice, including grouping nursing activities and reducing light and noise at night.
cycle2_result: Sleep quality mean 64 (SD 19.4), effect size 0.56; nurses' adherence exceeded the 80% thresholds by month 12.
other_findings: Measured at baseline, 1, 3, 6 and 12 months: month 1 mean 54, month 3 mean 64, month 6 mean 64. In total 120 patients surveyed and 150 observation audits.
authors: Ong KK; Khoo LM; Zhou Y; Tho PC
citation: Ong KK, Khoo LM, Zhou Y, Tho PC. Improving critical care patients' sleep quality in a surgical high-dependency unit: An evidence-based practice project. Worldviews Evid Based Nurs. 2022;19(2):166-168. doi:10.1111/wvn.12558. PMID: 35076157.

title: A human factors approach to quality improvement in oxygen prescribing.
standard: Oxygen prescribing quality standard of the National Asthma and COPD Audit Programme COPD Clinical Audit
finding: Oxygen prescription within the hospital electronic prescribing system showed poor compliance despite previous QI interventions (no figures given).
change: Functional resonance analysis method (FRAM), a human factors approach, used alongside QI methods to capture work-as-done and identify new potential interventions.
setting: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, hospital electronic prescribing system
cycle1_result: Oxygen prescription within the hospital electronic prescribing system showed poor compliance despite previous QI interventions (no figures given).
intervention: Functional resonance analysis method (FRAM), a human factors approach, used alongside QI methods to capture work-as-done and identify new potential interventions.
other_findings: Human factors tools may help bridge work-as-prescribed and work-as-done to support improvement and sustainability.
authors: Watson A; Rahul M; Dominic F; Higgs J; Williamson A; Turner A
citation: Watson A, Rahul M, Dominic F, Higgs J, Williamson A, Turner A. A human factors approach to quality improvement in oxygen prescribing. Clin Med (Lond). 2022;22(2):153-159. doi:10.7861/clinmed.2021-0164. PMID: 35105681.

title: Reducing omission of eye drops during hospital admission.
standard: NICE guideline on prescribing of eye drops during hospital admission
finding: Documentation of ocular diagnosis and eye drops in clerking 41%; eye drop reconciliation within 24 hours 45%; correct prescription 100%
change: Clinician education in mandatory induction sessions and ward posters as prompts
setting: Adult medical and surgical inpatients (Calderdale Royal Hospital / Nottingham)
cycle1_result: Documentation of ocular diagnosis and eye drops in clerking 41%; eye drop reconciliation within 24 hours 45%; correct prescription 100%
intervention: Clinician education in mandatory induction sessions and ward posters as prompts
cycle2_result: Documentation 65% (P = 0.008); reconciliation within 24 hours 75% (P = 0.0008); correct prescription 100%
other_findings: not reported
authors: Ho CS; Ting DSJ; Gogi D
journal: British journal of hospital medicine (London, England : 2005)
citation: Ho CS, Ting DSJ, Gogi D. Reducing omission of eye drops during hospital admission. Br J Hosp Med (Lond). 2022;83(1):1-7. doi:10.12968/hmed.2021.0577. PMID: 35129380.

title: The Value of Auditing Surgical Records in a Tertiary Hospital Setting.
standard: Surgical Tool for Auditing Records (STAR)
finding: Baseline STAR scores in 2016 (figures not given in abstract); 488 records evaluated across 2016 to 2021.
change: Electronic record entry system, personnel education and systematic auditing.
setting: General surgery department, Jordan University Hospital, Amman; tertiary hospital
cycle1_result: Baseline STAR scores in 2016 (figures not given in abstract); 488 records evaluated across 2016 to 2021.
intervention: Electronic record entry system, personnel education and systematic auditing.
cycle2_result: Total STAR scores improved steadily each year versus 2016 baseline, reaching the highest in 2021; all domains improved except anaesthesia records, which were already high.
other_findings: Largest improvements in Initial Clerking and Consent domains.
authors: Alqudah M; Aloqaily M; Rabadi A; Nimer A; Abdel Hafez S; Almomani A; Alkhlaifat NS; Aldurgham A; Al-Momani A; Fraij Z; Aloqaily W; Bani Abedelrahman L; AlShati A; Jabaiti S; Bani Hani A; Abu Abeeleh M

title: Audits of Antimicrobial Usage in a Tertiary Care Center in Hyderabad.
standard: Standard prescribing protocols and hospital antibiogram
finding: 95.45% of doctors attended sensitisation; 74.24% aware of prescription audits; 72.27% favoured antibiogram-based selection; 77.10% recommended sample collection before antibiotics; 63% of patients improved on antibiotics prescribed before culture report.
setting: 330-bed NABH-accredited tertiary care centre, Hyderabad
cycle1_result: 95.45% of doctors attended sensitisation; 74.24% aware of prescription audits; 72.27% favoured antibiogram-based selection; 77.10% recommended sample collection before antibiotics; 63% of patients improved on antibiotics prescribed before culture report.
other_findings: Use of antibiograms from cultures and environmental surveillance was followed well only after sensitising doctors.
authors: Jyothi L; K A; M S; Dara C; Sakthivadivel V; Sandepogu TS; Gaur A
citation: Jyothi L, K A, M S, Dara C, Sakthivadivel V, Sandepogu TS, et al.. Audits of Antimicrobial Usage in a Tertiary Care Center in Hyderabad. Cureus. 2022;14(1):e21125. doi:10.7759/cureus.21125. PMID: 35165580.

title: Image and report quality in non-obstetric ultrasound examinations undertaken by sonographers: Results of an audit of 3731 cases.
standard: Internal audit standard and externally set audit standards for sonographer non-obstetric ultrasound image and report quality
finding: Rolling audit: image and report quality exceeded externally set standards in all nine years (3186 patients); internal quality standard just failed to be met in the first five years but was achieved in all subsequent six years.
setting: Ultrasound department, Derriford Hospital, University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust (large university teaching hospital)
cycle1_result: Rolling audit: image and report quality exceeded externally set standards in all nine years (3186 patients); internal quality standard just failed to be met in the first five years but was achieved in all subsequent six years.
other_findings: Audit used for assurance and to direct individual professional development within a service with an active education programme.
authors: Freeman S; Cantin P; Gutteridge C; Williams P; Hamilton S; Lam Q; Dubbins P
citation: Freeman S, Cantin P, Gutteridge C, Williams P, Hamilton S, Lam Q, et al.. Image and report quality in non-obstetric ultrasound examinations undertaken by sonographers: Results of an audit of 3731 cases. Ultrasound. 2022;30(1):28-35. doi:10.1177/1742271x211033006. PMID: 35173776.

topic: Chronic disease monitoring in primary care
title: Using electronic medical record data to assess chronic kidney disease, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease testing, recognition and management as documented in Australian general practice: a cross-sectional analysis.
standard: Australian guidelines (or US guidelines if none) for risk factor assessment, diagnostic testing, monitoring and pharmacotherapy for CKD, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease
finding: BMI within timeframe 30%, blood pressure 46%; diagnostic testing as recommended 17% for CKD and 37% for T2D; guideline-recommended medications ranged from 44% (beta blockers in IHD) to 78% (antiplatelets/anticoagulants after ischaemic stroke).

cycle1_result: BMI within timeframe 30%, blood pressure 46%; diagnostic testing as recommended 17% for CKD and 37% for T2D; guideline-recommended medications ranged from 44% (beta blockers in IHD) to 78% (antiplatelets/anticoagulants after ischaemic stroke).
other_findings: Possible undiagnosed disease on pathology: CKD 6.7%, T2D 1.6%, familial hypercholesterolaemia 0.33%.

title: Assessing the quality of cardiac rehabilitation programs by measuring adherence to the Australian quality indicators.
standard: Australian Cardiovascular and Rehabilitation Association and Heart Foundation Cardiac Rehabilitation Quality Indicators
finding: Variable adherence to quality indicator measurement; median wait from discharge 27.0 days (IQR 19.3-46.0); completion of enrolled 76.9% country vs 56.5% metropolitan.

cycle1_result: Variable adherence to quality indicator measurement; median wait from discharge 27.0 days (IQR 19.3-46.0); completion of enrolled 76.9% country vs 56.5% metropolitan.

title: An audit into the timing of dental extractions pre-head and neck radiotherapy and the prevalence of osteoradionecrosis.
standard: Royal College of Surgeons guidelines: radiotherapy to commence ten days after dental extractions
finding: 125 assessed before radiotherapy, 102 (81.2%) needed extractions; 98.7% treated as per guidelines, 1.3% breached the ten-day protocol; ORN prevalence 1.3%.
setting: Department of Restorative Dentistry, Queen Alexandra Hospital, Portsmouth
cycle1_result: 125 assessed before radiotherapy, 102 (81.2%) needed extractions; 98.7% treated as per guidelines, 1.3% breached the ten-day protocol; ORN prevalence 1.3%.
other_findings: Timing of extractions showed no correlation with ORN over a minimum 20-month follow-up; further audit cycles recommended.
authors: Ward R; Kanani R; Romeed SA

title: Rates and Outcomes of Breast Lesions of Uncertain Malignant Potential (B3) benchmarked against the National Breast Screening Pathology Audit; Improving Performance in a High Volume Screening Unit.
standard: National Breast Screening Pathology Audit benchmark B3 rate
finding: B3 rate 12.4% (30% above national average); PPV 7.7% (9.7% with atypia).
change: Consensus microscopic review of AIDEP cases against published criteria
setting: Breast screening pathology, Royal Free London Foundation Trust
cycle1_result: B3 rate 12.4% (30% above national average); PPV 7.7% (9.7% with atypia).
intervention: Consensus microscopic review of AIDEP cases against published criteria
cycle2_result: B3 rate 9.11%, more in line with national standards.
other_findings: On review AIDEP was confirmed in only 66%, 17% were downgraded and 16% did not reach consensus.
authors: Sheikh SE; Rathbone M; Chaudhary K; Joshi A; Lee J; Muthukumar S; Mylona E; Roxanis I; Rees J

topic: Antibiotic prescribing in upper respiratory tract infection
title: Delayed antibiotic prescribing to reduce antibiotic use: an urgent care practice change.
standard: CDC adult URI treatment guidelines for antibiotic use
finding: Chart audits showed antibiotics routinely prescribed for URI without patient instruction; comparative group n = 598.
change: Implementation of CDC URI guidelines with delayed antibiotic prescribing and follow-up phone calls 10 days after discharge.
setting: Urgent care clinic, central Arizona
cycle1_result: Chart audits showed antibiotics routinely prescribed for URI without patient instruction; comparative group n = 598.
intervention: Implementation of CDC URI guidelines with delayed antibiotic prescribing and follow-up phone calls 10 days after discharge.
cycle2_result: Antibiotic usage rates decreased by 12% in 30 days (U = 247, p = 0.023).
other_findings: High patient satisfaction was maintained; most urgent care sites lacked an antibiotic stewardship plan.
authors: Tonazzi S; Prenovost L; Scheuermann S
citation: Tonazzi S, Prenovost L, Scheuermann S. Delayed antibiotic prescribing to reduce antibiotic use: an urgent care practice change. BMJ Open Qual. 2022;11(1):e001513. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2021-001513. PMID: 35264330.

title: Review DebrIeF: a collaborative distributed leadership approach to "hot debrief" after cardiac arrest in the emergency department - a quality improvement project.
standard: Hot debrief after cardiac arrest (American Heart Association recommendation; Royal College QI requirements)
finding: Audit identified zero hot debriefs occurring in 2019 (0%).
change: Four PDSA cycles (March 2020 to September 2021) using staff surveys and interviews to co-design and implement an ED hot debrief tool with a nurse-led distributed leadership approach.
setting: Emergency Department, Doncaster Royal Infirmary, Doncaster and Bassetlaw Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
cycle1_result: Audit identified zero hot debriefs occurring in 2019 (0%).
intervention: Four PDSA cycles (March 2020 to September 2021) using staff surveys and interviews to co-design and implement an ED hot debrief tool with a nurse-led distributed leadership approach.
cycle2_result: 5 of 12 cardiac arrests had a hot debrief (42% increase from 0%).
other_findings: Six months on there were still inconsistencies and barriers; second survey (n = 58) suggested doctors were less convinced of benefits than nurses.
authors: James S; Subedi P; Indrasena BSH; Aylott J
citation: James S, Subedi P, Indrasena BSH, Aylott J. Review DebrIeF: a collaborative distributed leadership approach to "hot debrief" after cardiac arrest in the emergency department - a quality improvement project. title: Evaluating peripheral intravascular catheter insertion, maintenance and removal practices in small hospitals using a standardized audit tool.
standard: Standardised PIVC audit tool for insertion, maintenance and removal practices
finding: 22.6% did not report a visual infusion phlebitis score at least daily; 48% did not document daily dressing assessment.

cycle1_result: 22.6% did not report a visual infusion phlebitis score at least daily; 48% did not document daily dressing assessment.
other_findings: 57.6% inserted on wards; removal reasons: no longer required 63%, phlebitis 4.8%; no bloodstream infections.

citation: Hoskins A, Worth LJ, Malloy MJ, Smith M, Atkins S, Bennett N. Evaluating peripheral intravascular catheter insertion, maintenance and removal practices in small hospitals using a standardized audit tool. Nurs Open. 2022;9(3):1912-1917. doi:10.1002/nop2.1176. PMID: 35274830.

title: Quality Improvement Within a Mental Health Setting: Alcohol Detoxification.
standard: NICE guidelines on alcohol detoxification (history, physical examination including Wernicke's screening, vital signs, liver tests, breath alcohol, standardised withdrawal assessment, chlordiazepoxide and thiamine prescribing); POMH-UK audit
finding: First cycle as part of POMH-UK audit showed greater compliance than other services; breath alcohol level documented in 79% and CIWA in 39% (before final cycle).

cycle1_result: First cycle as part of POMH-UK audit showed greater compliance than other services; breath alcohol level documented in 79% and CIWA in 39% (before final cycle).

authors: Doody E; Malone A; Gallagher B; Hopkins K; Weir D; Nolan M; Kowalska-Beda P; Naughton M
citation: Doody E, Malone A, Gallagher B, Hopkins K, Weir D, Nolan M, et al.. Quality Improvement Within a Mental Health Setting: Alcohol Detoxification. Ir Med J. 2022;115(1):516. PMID: 35279050.

title: An Audit of the Technical Quality and Iatrogenic Errors of Root Canal Treatment by Undergraduate Dental Students at the University of Sharjah.

cycle1_result: Acceptable quality in 183/480 teeth (38.1%); 4th-year students 41.9% vs 5th-year 27.4% (p = 0.004).

title: Audit of documentation accompanying referred maternity cases to a referral hospital in northern Ghana: a mixed-methods study.
standard: Completion of maternity referral forms
finding: Completion rates of referral forms reported (figures not given in abstract); 83.9% referred for advanced care, 8.3% for lack of logistics.
setting: Four units (antenatal, antenatal emergency, labour, neonatal intensive care) of a referral hospital in northern Ghana

intervention: Proposed electronic reminders, structured antipsychotic monitoring template, teaching for medical staff and re-audit in 6 to 12 months

topic: Falls risk screening and multifactorial assessment
title: Falls Risk Assessment Compliance and Outcomes in Psychiatry of Old Age Inpatient Department
standard: NICE CG161: falls risk assessment within 24 hours of admission with interventions for identified risks

change: Education for team members on timely and accurate falls risk assessment

cycle1_result: 4 of 5 patients (80%) assessed within 24 hours with risks addressed within 48 hours; clinical documentation present for all (100%); 4 falls recorded, all documented (100%)
intervention: Education for team members on timely and accurate falls risk assessment
other_findings: Cycle one was judged compliant, but documentation quality and consistency needed improvement. Cycle 2 data collection was under way.

title: Monitoring Troponin I and CRP During Clozapine Titration: Assessing Adherence to Myocarditis Protocols
standard: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines and Ronaldson algorithm: baseline and weekly troponin and CRP during the first four weeks of clozapine titration
finding: Baseline troponin and CRP documented in 80%, baseline ECG in 90%; 5 (50%) had mildly raised troponin (>3 but <13 ng/L), 80% of these had repeat troponin testing; no suspected myocarditis
change: Recommendations to align local practice with Ronaldson and Maudsley protocols using locally agreed reference ranges, to be added to local policy; re-audit planned
setting: Swallownest Court general adult psychiatry inpatient wards, Rotherham Doncaster and South Humber NHS Foundation Trust
cycle1_result: Baseline troponin and CRP documented in 80%, baseline ECG in 90%; 5 (50%) had mildly raised troponin (>3 but <13 ng/L), 80% of these had repeat troponin testing; no suspected myocarditis
intervention: Recommendations to align local practice with Ronaldson and Maudsley protocols using locally agreed reference ranges, to be added to local policy; re-audit planned
other_findings: Repeat troponin tests were often triggered by acute coronary syndrome reference ranges rather than myocarditis thresholds. CRP rose in four patients, two from non-cardiac causes.
authors: Chowdhury T; Martin A

standard: Pregnancy test and gynaecological history for female admissions of reproductive age within the first 2 weeks of admission

cycle1_result: Pregnancy test within 2 weeks 14.3% (4/28); asked about chance of pregnancy 7.14% (1/28); last menstrual period asked in 1 patient; contraception and sexual activity asked in none; cervical screening up to date 53.57% (15/28)
intervention: Proposed posters, presentations and changes to prescribing software; re-audit planned
other_findings: not reported
authors: Osman F; Islam I; Hall R; Andrews H

title: Managing Memory - Optimising Anti-Dementia Medication Prescribing in an Inpatient Setting
standard: Trust and Maudsley prescribing guidelines for indication, dose titration and physical health monitoring; target at least 90% adherence per domain
finding: 7/20 (35%) candidates for inpatient-initiated anti-dementia medication; of 6 offered, 5 clearly indicated (83%); all titrated per guideline; physical health monitoring completed in 5 (83%)
change: Raising staff awareness, disseminating results and visible audit reminders on ward lists

cycle1_result: 7/20 (35%) candidates for inpatient-initiated anti-dementia medication; of 6 offered, 5 clearly indicated (83%); all titrated per guideline; physical health monitoring completed in 5 (83%)
intervention: Raising staff awareness, disseminating results and visible audit reminders on ward lists
cycle2_result: 6 (30%) candidates, only 4 prescribed an indicated drug (67%); all inpatient-initiated medications titrated and monitored to standard
other_findings: The target was met in two of three domains by cycle 2 but indication remained below standard. Pre-admission anti-dementia prescriptions were 65% and 55%.

title: Screening for the impact of social media use on self-harm crisis presentations in children and adolescents - are we adhering to NICE guidelines?
standard: NICE 2022 self-harm guideline: psychosocial assessment includes enquiry about social media, its use to connect with others and its effect on mental health
finding: Social media enquiry 72%; social media used to connect with others 14%; impact on mental health 8%
change: Planned presentation of results, training and re-audit

cycle1_result: Social media enquiry 72%; social media used to connect with others 14%; impact on mental health 8%
intervention: Planned presentation of results, training and re-audit
other_findings: Of those asked, 97% used social media and all 4 asked about impact reported a negative effect on mental health. Self-poisoning was the commonest type of self-harm (48%).

title: Improving the management of Insomnia in Community General Adult Mental Health Care
standard: National guidance on insomnia management (Donaldson et al. 2009; NICE CKS 2025): sleep hygiene, CBT-i and appropriate hypnotic use
finding: Insomnia prevalence 58%; sleep hygiene advice 36% of relevant patients; CBT-i strategies 11%; combination hypnotics 15%
change: Education programme for the clinical team on sleep physiology, guidelines and CBT-i, plus a simplified sleep management algorithm
setting: Community general adult mental health team, South West London and St George's Mental Health NHS Trust
cycle1_period: Patients seen over the previous five months
cycle1_result: Insomnia prevalence 58%; sleep hygiene advice 36% of relevant patients; CBT-i strategies 11%; combination hypnotics 15%
intervention: Education programme for the clinical team on sleep physiology, guidelines and CBT-i, plus a simplified sleep management algorithm
cycle2_result: Insomnia prevalence 63%; sleep hygiene advice 45%; CBT-i strategies 27%; combination hypnotics 8%
other_findings: CBT-i remained underused despite being first line. Zopiclone and promethazine were the most used hypnotics.
authors: Heslop J
journal: European psychiatry : the journal of the Association of European Psychiatrists
citation: Heslop J. Improving the management of Insomnia in Community General Adult Mental Health Care. Eur Psychiatry. ;69(Suppl 1):S279-S280.

title: Out of Town Meeting of the Ulster Paediatric Society, Friday 8th and Saturday 9th May 2009
standard: Regional hypopack protocol: samples analysed and reported, taken while the patient is hypoglycaemic and before dextrose, and reports filed in charts
finding: 35% of patients hypoglycaemic (<2.6 mmol/L) when sampled; 54% sampled before dextrose; 35% of laboratory reports missing from charts
change: Redesigned request form, updated protocol and a summative report, introduced April 2006 with presentations to regional centres
setting: Regional hypoglycaemia screen (hypopack) service across A&E departments, children's wards and neonatal units, Belfast Health and Social Care Trust (meeting abstract)
cycle1_result: 35% of patients hypoglycaemic (<2.6 mmol/L) when sampled; 54% sampled before dextrose; 35% of laboratory reports missing from charts
intervention: Redesigned request form, updated protocol and a summative report, introduced April 2006 with presentations to regional centres
cycle2_result: 49% hypoglycaemic when sampled; 64% sampled before dextrose; 21% of insulin samples rejected as haemolysed; 35% of reports still missing from charts
other_findings: The record is a meeting programme with several other abstracts, including a congenital heart disease delivery audit and a fluid electrolyte audit. Intrauterine growth restriction and fasting due to gastroenteritis were the commonest causes of hypoglycaemia.
authors: Lang T; Cardy D; Leslie H; Sheridan B; Carson D; Loughrey C
citation: Lang T, Cardy D, Leslie H, Sheridan B, Carson D, Loughrey C. Out of Town Meeting of the Ulster Paediatric Society, Friday 8th and Saturday 9th May 2009. Ulster Med J. 2009;78(3):194-199.

title: Awareness of difficult airway equipment on the ICU
standard: 100% of clinicians aware of location and contents of the difficult airway trolley; 100% of anaesthetists trained in difficult airway equipment
finding: 100% aware of the trolley; 35% had read the contents folder; 90% could name the equipment; 70% confident to use it unaided; 28% not airway trained
change: Designated consultant teaching at quarterly induction, simulation and mannequin training, case-based teaching and airway proficiency assessments at induction
setting: ICU, Royal Liverpool University Hospital
cycle1_result: 100% aware of the trolley; 35% had read the contents folder; 90% could name the equipment; 70% confident to use it unaided; 28% not airway trained
intervention: Designated consultant teaching at quarterly induction, simulation and mannequin training, case-based teaching and airway proficiency assessments at induction
cycle2_result: 100% aware of the equipment; 60% confident in its use; 100% airway trained
other_findings: Requests for an ODP at unplanned intubations rose from 50% to 80%.
authors: Wozniak A; Iyer A
citation: Wozniak A, Iyer A. Awareness of difficult airway equipment on the ICU. Crit Care. 2012;16(Suppl 1):P525-P525.

topic: Targeted temperature management after cardiac arrest
title: Introduction of an external noninvasive cooling device for effective implementation of Intensive Care Society standards post cardiac arrest
standard: Intensive Care Society standards: cooling to 32 to 34°C for 12 to 24 hours after ROSC
finding: Effectively cooled within 4 hours 33%; maintained in target range over 24 hours 57%; mean CPC at ICU discharge 3.4
change: Introduction of an external noninvasive cooling device (CritiCool)
setting: Critical care unit, University College Hospital London
cycle1_result: Effectively cooled within 4 hours 33%; maintained in target range over 24 hours 57%; mean CPC at ICU discharge 3.4
intervention: Introduction of an external noninvasive cooling device (CritiCool)
cycle2_result: Effectively cooled within 4 hours 57%; maintained in target range 70%; mean CPC 2.3
other_findings: not reported

title: Impact of introducing guidelines for thrombolysis of submassive pulmonary embolism at a large UK teaching hospital
standard: New local guideline allowing thrombolysis for massive and submassive PE
finding: Previous guidelines suggested considering thrombolysis in only seven patients in 6 months
change: New local guideline for thrombolysis of submassive and massive PE introduced March 2013
setting: University Hospitals Southampton NHS Foundation Trust, large teaching hospital
cycle1_result: Previous guidelines suggested considering thrombolysis in only seven patients in 6 months
intervention: New local guideline for thrombolysis of submassive and massive PE introduced March 2013
cycle2_result: 46 patients with massive or submassive PE (32% of all PEs); thrombolysis given to 2, but 6 had no contraindications
other_findings: Barriers were late recognition of submassive PE and poor awareness of the guideline change.
authors: Misselbrook G
citation: Misselbrook G. Impact of introducing guidelines for thrombolysis of submassive pulmonary embolism at a large UK teaching hospital. Crit Care. 2015;19(Suppl 1):P324-P324. doi:10.1186/cc14404.

title: Written communication for itu discharges: a quality improvement project
standard: NICE clinical guidelines 50 and 83 domains for discharge summaries
finding: Frequent omissions: patient demographics (10%), doctor's designation (8%), bleep number (68%), plain-English summary for relatives (18%), relevant investigations (35%), monitoring plan on the ward (45%)
change: Electronic discharge summary template with mandatory NICE-based headings and prompts
setting: ITU, Northampton General Hospital
cycle1_result: Frequent omissions: patient demographics (10%), doctor's designation (8%), bleep number (68%), plain-English summary for relatives (18%), relevant investigations (35%), monitoring plan on the ward (45%)
intervention: Electronic discharge summary template with mandatory NICE-based headings and prompts
cycle2_result: Legal aspects almost 100% compliant; reason for admission 99%; diagnosis 85%
other_findings: Pending investigations, nutrition plan, infection status, limitations of treatment and information for relatives now appear on summaries.
authors: Bendel D; Gardner H; Outram M
citation: Bendel D, Gardner H, Outram M. Written communication for itu discharges: a quality improvement project. Intensive Care Med Exp. 2015;3(Suppl 1).

topic: Soft tissue tumour referral and diagnosis
title: Histopathological diagnostic discrepancies in soft tissue tumours referred to a specialist centre: reassessment in the era of ancillary molecular diagnosis.
standard: NICE and RCPath recommendation that suspected soft tissue sarcomas are referred for specialist pathology review; discrepancy rates compared with the unit's 2005 audit
finding: Diagnostic agreement 73.4%; discrepancy 27.5% (15.7% minor, 10.9% major); 5% of discrepant cases benign-malignant discordances
change: No local intervention; in the interval referral guidance was widely adopted and ancillary molecular testing became routine
setting: Sarcoma Unit, Department of Histopathology, The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust, tertiary cancer centre
cycle1_result: Diagnostic agreement 73.4%; discrepancy 27.5% (15.7% minor, 10.9% major); 5% of discrepant cases benign-malignant discordances
intervention: No local intervention; in the interval referral guidance was widely adopted and ancillary molecular testing became routine
cycle2_result: Diagnostic agreement 250 (71.8%); 57 (16.4%) major and 41 (11.8%) minor discrepancies; 23 benign-malignant discrepancies (23.5% of discrepancies)
other_findings: Molecular tests contributed to only 3 major and 4 minor discrepancies; most discrepancies were interpretational. The authors support national guidance that all suspected soft tissue tumours are referred to a specialist unit.
authors: Thway K; Wang J; Mubako T; Fisher C
citation: Thway K, Wang J, Mubako T, Fisher C. Histopathological diagnostic discrepancies in soft tissue tumours referred to a specialist centre: reassessment in the era of ancillary molecular diagnosis. Sarcoma. 2014;2014:686902. doi:10.1155/2014/686902. PMID: 25165418.

title: An implementation program targeted at non-physician, anaesthesia assistants improves the quality of laryngeal mask anaesthesia.
standard: LMA cuff pressure within the manufacturers' recommended limit of <60 cmH2O, measured by manometer
finding: Only 4 (5%) cuff pressures were within the recommended <60 cmH2O; 57 (63%) exceeded the manometer scale (>120 cmH2O); 25 (27%) reported sore throat.
change: Results presented to anaesthetists and anaesthetic assistants; manometers bought for every theatre; education and in-theatre demonstration for anaesthetic assistants on measuring and adjusting cuff pressure.
setting: Theatres, University College London Hospitals (UCLH)
cycle1_result: Only 4 (5%) cuff pressures were within the recommended <60 cmH2O; 57 (63%) exceeded the manometer scale (>120 cmH2O); 25 (27%) reported sore throat.
intervention: Results presented to anaesthetists and anaesthetic assistants; manometers bought for every theatre; education and in-theatre demonstration for anaesthetic assistants on measuring and adjusting cuff pressure.
cycle2_result: LMA pressures within recommended limits rose to 43%; pressures exceeding the manometer fell to 16%; pharyngolaryngeal morbidity 11% in the 45 patients whose pressure was reduced to normal (P=0.001).
other_findings: Adherence remained suboptimal, with staff turnover and agency assistants cited as barriers; manometry was adopted as standard of care at University College Hospital.
authors: Reed I; Walker E; Oliver Rose B
citation: Reed I, Walker E, Oliver Rose B. An implementation program targeted at non-physician, anaesthesia assistants improves the quality of laryngeal mask anaesthesia. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2014;2(2):u201077.w693. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u201077.w693. PMID: 26734211.

title: Improving hospital weekend handover: a user-centered, standardised approach.
standard: Royal College of Physicians handover guidance (minimum of 3 patient identifiers, ceiling of care, task urgency, assigned team member)
finding: 12 different pro formas in use; 87% had 3 patient identifiers; 1% documented ceiling of care; 0% documented task urgency; 63% had a named team member for the task
change: Standardised weekend handover pro forma based on RCP guidance, launched with a teaching session, trust email and ward visits
setting: Department of general medicine, acute teaching hospital, Brighton and Sussex University Hospitals NHS Trust
cycle1_result: 12 different pro formas in use; 87% had 3 patient identifiers; 1% documented ceiling of care; 0% documented task urgency; 63% had a named team member for the task
intervention: Standardised weekend handover pro forma based on RCP guidance, launched with a teaching session, trust email and ward visits
cycle2_result: 100% uptake of the single pro forma; 98% had 3 patient identifiers; 60% documented ceiling of care; 88% documented task urgency; 100% had a named team member
other_findings: At 4 weeks (76 patients): 95% identifiers, 45% ceiling of care, 67% urgency, 97% team member. 88% of surveyed doctors felt the new pro forma improved safety; electronic handover software and handover teaching at induction followed.
authors: Mehra A; Henein C
citation: Mehra A, Henein C. Improving hospital weekend handover: a user-centered, standardised approach. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2014;2(2):u202861.w1655. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u202861.w1655. PMID: 26734248.

title: Improving the quality of patient handover on a surgical ward.
standard: Royal College of Surgeons of England guidelines on surgical patient handover (minimum data set)
finding: 15% of patients handed over from CAU to ward FY1; 0% of handovers included the full RCSEng minimum data set
change: Handover tool based on RCSEng guidance attached to the notes and signed by both FY1s, policy that handover occurs after senior review, a named ward FY1 for new admissions, and teaching
setting: Combined Assessment Unit and surgical ward, Perth Royal Infirmary, district general hospital
cycle1_result: 15% of patients handed over from CAU to ward FY1; 0% of handovers included the full RCSEng minimum data set
intervention: Handover tool based on RCSEng guidance attached to the notes and signed by both FY1s, policy that handover occurs after senior review, a named ward FY1 for new admissions, and teaching
cycle2_result: 45% of patients handed over; 100% of handovers contained all recommended information
other_findings: At baseline FY1s first learnt of 48% of new admissions on the ward round, and 60% of patients whose SEWS score rose between CAU and the ward were not handed over.
authors: Bradley A
citation: Bradley A. Improving the quality of patient handover on a surgical ward. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2014;3(1):u201797.w1958. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u201797.w1958. PMID: 26734304.

title: Evaluating the Quality of Medical Documentation at a University Teaching Hospital.
standard: NHS Litigation Authority record keeping standards, CQC essential standards and Oxford University Hospitals documentation guidelines (VTE assessment within 6 hours, clear plan, postoperative instructions, senior present documented, contemporaneous entries)
finding: VTE assessment within 6 hours 80% (available in 100%); plan and postoperative instructions 100%; contemporaneous entries 75%; consultant presence documented 80%
change: Findings presented at the departmental audit meeting to raise awareness of contemporaneous documentation and recording the most senior person present
setting: University teaching hospital (inpatient notes; presented at the Nordic Orthopaedic Federation)
cycle1_result: VTE assessment within 6 hours 80% (available in 100%); plan and postoperative instructions 100%; contemporaneous entries 75%; consultant presence documented 80%
intervention: Findings presented at the departmental audit meeting to raise awareness of contemporaneous documentation and recording the most senior person present
other_findings: Second cycle at 6 months: contemporaneous entries 80%, consultant presence 90%. Junior doctor presence was hard to establish and EPR timestamps make contemporaneous entry hard to judge.
authors: Ridyard E; Street E
citation: Ridyard E, Street E. Evaluating the Quality of Medical Documentation at a University Teaching Hospital. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2015;4(1):u208052.w3253. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u208052.w3253. PMID: 26734328.

title: Improving medical handover at the weekend: a quality improvement project.
standard: Royal College of Physicians medical handover guidelines
finding: Doctor survey: 12% used the electronic system for weekend handover; 89% found sorting jobs time consuming; 67% handed jobs meant for another grade; 41% knew who to hand weekend discharges to; safety score 3.18/5
change: New dedicated electronic handover database with a proforma, earlier structured Friday handover meeting chaired by a registrar with SBAR and a register, plus teaching, grand round and email from the medical director
setting: Medical wards, Broomfield Hospital, Mid Essex Hospital Services NHS Trust
cycle1_result: Doctor survey: 12% used the electronic system for weekend handover; 89% found sorting jobs time consuming; 67% handed jobs meant for another grade; 41% knew who to hand weekend discharges to; safety score 3.18/5
intervention: New dedicated electronic handover database with a proforma, earlier structured Friday handover meeting chaired by a registrar with SBAR and a register, plus teaching, grand round and email from the medical director
cycle2_result: 100% used the electronic system; 47% found sorting jobs time consuming; 37% handed jobs for another grade; 89% knew who to hand discharges to; safety score 3.84/5
other_findings: Measures were from doctor questionnaires. Registrar attendance at the meeting and inappropriate or poorly explained jobs remained problems.
authors: Michael E; Patel C
citation: Michael E, Patel C. Improving medical handover at the weekend: a quality improvement project. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2015;4(1):u207153.w2899. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u207153.w2899. PMID: 26734385.

title: A multifaceted approach to prevention of delirium on intensive care.
standard: NICE CG103 delirium guidance; delirium rate compared with PRE-DELIRIC predicted rate (39%)
finding: Level 3 ICU patients: delirium at first assessment 65%, at any time 70% (16/23); 87% exposed to deliriogenic drugs
change: Two PDSA programmes: delirium teaching, lighter sedation with short-acting agents and daily sedation breaks, redesigned drug booklets and charts, then unit refurbishment with more natural light and clocks, dexmedetomidine and chart prompts for delirium assessment
setting: General adult critical care unit, Manchester Royal Infirmary
cycle1_result: Level 3 ICU patients: delirium at first assessment 65%, at any time 70% (16/23); 87% exposed to deliriogenic drugs
intervention: Two PDSA programmes: delirium teaching, lighter sedation with short-acting agents and daily sedation breaks, redesigned drug booklets and charts, then unit refurbishment with more natural light and clocks, dexmedetomidine and chart prompts for delirium assessment
cycle2_result: Delirium at first assessment 15%, at any time 29% (predicted 39%); 70% exposed to deliriogenic drugs
other_findings: After the first PDSA cycle (85 patients) delirium was 16% at first assessment and 44% at any time; the second cycle added less, suggesting a plateau.
authors: Hanison J; Conway D
citation: Hanison J, Conway D. A multifaceted approach to prevention of delirium on intensive care. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2015;4(1):u209656.w4000. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u209656.w4000. PMID: 26734390.

title: Are we meeting current standards in medicines reconciliation? A study in a District General Hospital.
standard: NICE and Scottish Patient Safety Programme: 95% of patients to have medicines reconciliation within 24 hours of admission
finding: 46% reconciled on admission and 77% within 24 hours (abstract states 49% and 75%)
change: Emergency Care Summary access for junior doctors plus lunchtime teaching and email reinforcement
setting: Acute surgical receiving ward, Hairmyres Hospital, NHS Lanarkshire, district general hospital
cycle1_result: 46% reconciled on admission and 77% within 24 hours (abstract states 49% and 75%)
intervention: Emergency Care Summary access for junior doctors plus lunchtime teaching and email reinforcement
cycle2_result: Third cycle: 57% completed on admission and 84% at 24 hours; 89% had a complete medication history
other_findings: Second cycle showed 62% on admission and 86% at 24 hours with 93% accurate history; performance slipped at the third cycle and never reached 95%. Six patients were lost to follow up and three discharged within 24 hours at baseline.
authors: Iddles E; Williamson A; Bradley A; Khan K
citation: Iddles E, Williamson A, Bradley A, Khan K. Are we meeting current standards in medicines reconciliation? A study in a District General Hospital. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2015;4(1):u207508.w3002. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u207508.w3002. PMID: 26734398.

title: Improving the management of sepsis in a district general hospital by implementing the 'Sepsis Six' recommendations.
standard: Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines and Sepsis Six bundle; antibiotics, IV fluids and oxygen within one hour of initial assessment
finding: 16 of 55 (29%) had antibiotics, IV fluids with or without oxygen within 1 hour; lactate measured in 10 (18%); blood cultures in 18 (33%); urine output monitoring in 15 (27%); 35% received 4-6 bundle elements.
change: Sepsis Six pathway and posters; education workshops for ED staff, junior doctors and ward nurses; designated sepsis assistants; laminated Sepsis Six photo on ED phlebotomy trolleys; request for an extra ED consultant.
setting: 130-bed district general hospital (ED and general wards), South Canterbury DHB
cycle1_result: 16 of 55 (29%) had antibiotics, IV fluids with or without oxygen within 1 hour; lactate measured in 10 (18%); blood cultures in 18 (33%); urine output monitoring in 15 (27%); 35% received 4-6 bundle elements.
intervention: Sepsis Six pathway and posters; education workshops for ED staff, junior doctors and ward nurses; designated sepsis assistants; laminated Sepsis Six photo on ED phlebotomy trolleys; request for an extra ED consultant.
cycle2_result: 25 of 40 (63%) had antibiotics, fluids with or without oxygen within 1 hour; lactate 10 (25%); blood cultures 25 (63%), 96% before antibiotics; urine output monitoring 17 (43%); 66% received 4-6 bundle elements.
other_findings: A 3-month re-audit (n = 71) showed 52% within 1 hour. Time to clinician review did not improve (47 to 44 minutes) and in-hospital mortality rose from 2% to 10%, possibly due to winter re-audits.
authors: Kumar P; Jordan M; Caesar J; Miller S
citation: Kumar P, Jordan M, Caesar J, Miller S. Improving the management of sepsis in a district general hospital by implementing the 'Sepsis Six' recommendations. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2015;4(1):u207871.w4032. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u207871.w4032. PMID: 26734403.

title: A simple prioritisation system to improve the electronic handover.
standard: GMC and BMA/NPSA safe handover guidance: unstable patients known to seniors, tasks prioritised and unstable patients reviewed
finding: FY1 questionnaire: 38.5% felt handover was safe; 7.1% had sufficient time to complete the ward round; 15.4% could identify and prioritise unwell patients; 30.8% could identify outstanding jobs
change: Traffic light prioritisation categories (including weekend discharge and weekend admissions) added to the electronic weekend handover on EPR, publicised by posters, email and FY1 induction
setting: Trauma and orthopaedic department, King's College Hospital, major trauma centre, London
cycle1_result: FY1 questionnaire: 38.5% felt handover was safe; 7.1% had sufficient time to complete the ward round; 15.4% could identify and prioritise unwell patients; 30.8% could identify outstanding jobs
intervention: Traffic light prioritisation categories (including weekend discharge and weekend admissions) added to the electronic weekend handover on EPR, publicised by posters, email and FY1 induction
cycle2_result: Improvement sustained across all parameters but smaller than immediately after the change (detailed figures only in supplementary table)
other_findings: Immediately after the change (8 responders): safe handover 100%, time to complete ward round 50%, time for bleeps 100%, prioritising unwell patients 100%, identifying outstanding jobs 87.5%. Measures were FY1 opinions from questionnaires.
authors: Ah-Kye L; Moore M
citation: Ah-Kye L, Moore M. A simple prioritisation system to improve the electronic handover. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2015;4(1):u205385.w4127. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u205385.w4127. PMID: 26734404.

title: Improving cranial ultrasound scanning strategy in neonates.
standard: Consultant-agreed scanning schedule and local documentation standards; 100% of infants scanned to schedule and 100% of key documentation fields completed
finding: 52% of preterm (93 scans) and 44% of term (9 scans) scans performed to schedule; preterm reports with time documented 75% and scanning doctor's name 92%; no comment on IVH in 16% of preterm scans
change: Departmental audit meeting education (PDSA 1, no real improvement), then a local cranial ultrasound guideline, a documentation template in every set of notes, posters, email and a one-minute-wonder board (PDSA 2)
setting: Tertiary neonatal intensive care unit, Queen Alexandra Hospital, Portsmouth
cycle1_result: 52% of preterm (93 scans) and 44% of term (9 scans) scans performed to schedule; preterm reports with time documented 75% and scanning doctor's name 92%; no comment on IVH in 16% of preterm scans
intervention: Departmental audit meeting education (PDSA 1, no real improvement), then a local cranial ultrasound guideline, a documentation template in every set of notes, posters, email and a one-minute-wonder board (PDSA 2)
cycle2_result: 74% of preterm and 100% of term scans performed to schedule; 100% had doctor's name and time of scan documented; 100% of preterm reports documented IVH
other_findings: Documentation of when the next scan was due stayed poor (missing in 37% of preterm and 20% of term scans) and signature rates fell because the template lacked a signature box.
authors: Bray L
citation: Bray L. Improving cranial ultrasound scanning strategy in neonates. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2016;5(1):u210346.w4219. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u210346.w4219. PMID: 27096095.

title: Improving the provision of pregnancy care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women: a continuous quality improvement initiative.
standard: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines for Antenatal Care: screening and counselling for smoking, alcohol, nutrition, physical activity and food security, and folate before 20 weeks
finding: Screened for cigarette use 73%; cessation advice 52%; screened for alcohol 65%; brief alcohol counselling 51%; nutrition counselling 41%; food security counselling 4.8%; physical activity counselling 20%; folate before 20 weeks 28%.
change: Continuous quality improvement cycles: systems assessment and health record audits, with each centre setting priorities and developing its own system improvement strategies, supported by One21seventy tools and facilitators.
setting: 50 primary health care centres in predominantly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities (ABCD National Research Partnership) across five Australian states and territories
cycle1_result: Screened for cigarette use 73%; cessation advice 52%; screened for alcohol 65%; brief alcohol counselling 51%; nutrition counselling 41%; food security counselling 4.8%; physical activity counselling 20%; folate before 20 weeks 28%.
intervention: Continuous quality improvement cycles: systems assessment and health record audits, with each centre setting priorities and developing its own system improvement strategies, supported by One21seventy tools and facilitators.
cycle2_result: Screened for cigarette use 95% (OR 11); cessation advice 73%; screened for alcohol 83%; brief alcohol counselling 71%; nutrition counselling 65%; food security counselling 9.1%; physical activity counselling 15%; folate before 20 weeks 34%.
other_findings: After cycle 1 (n = 758) cigarette screening was 90%; four CQI cycles in total. Better self-rated organisational systems were associated with more alcohol screening, nutrition counselling and folate prescription; lifestyle counselling and folate remained poor.
authors: Gibson-Helm ME; Rumbold AR; Teede HJ; Ranasinha S; Bailie RS; Boyle JA
citation: Gibson-Helm ME, Rumbold AR, Teede HJ, Ranasinha S, Bailie RS, Boyle JA. Improving the provision of pregnancy care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women: a continuous quality improvement initiative. BMC Pregnancy Childbirth. 2016;16:118. doi:10.1186/s12884-016-0892-1. PMID: 27221473.

title: Improving the quality of handover in a liaison psychiatry team.
standard: Locally agreed minimum handover data set (patient identifiers, location, referrer, reason for referral, priority, risk, pending tasks, clinician name and signature)
finding: Overall completeness 40%; hospital number 2%; risk 22%; priority of task 13%; clinician name 29%; signature 15%
change: Education and a written handout at induction (no consistent improvement), then a handover proforma sticker, later a printed handover book
setting: Liaison psychiatry service at King's College Hospital, South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust
cycle1_result: Overall completeness 40%; hospital number 2%; risk 22%; priority of task 13%; clinician name 29%; signature 15%
intervention: Education and a written handout at induction (no consistent improvement), then a handover proforma sticker, later a printed handover book
cycle2_result: Overall completeness 78%; hospital number 48%; risk 53%; priority 59%; pending tasks 100%; clinician name 97%; signature 97%
other_findings: After education alone completeness was 34% to 46%; immediately after the proforma it was 71% and 72% at two months. Recording of risk and contact numbers stayed relatively poor.
authors: Brook J; Amaro Calcia M
citation: Brook J, Amaro Calcia M. Improving the quality of handover in a liaison psychiatry team. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2016;5(1):u206492.w3442. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u206492.w3442. PMID: 27335644.

title: The use of a pro forma to improve quality in clerking vascular surgery patients.
standard: Royal College of Physicians 2009 standards for admission clerking documentation
finding: Presenting complaint absent in 19%; past surgical history absent in 45%; drug history 72%, doses and frequency 41%, allergy status 75%; family history 19%; systems enquiry 12%; vascular examination 59%, pulses 46%; observations 31%; VTE assessment 73%
change: Clerking pro forma based on RCP guidance (with AMTS, VTE, ABPI, investigations and nil-by-mouth sections), junior doctor education and a named FY1 lead per cohort
setting: Vascular surgery ward, large tertiary referral centre, Barts Health NHS Trust
cycle1_result: Presenting complaint absent in 19%; past surgical history absent in 45%; drug history 72%, doses and frequency 41%, allergy status 75%; family history 19%; systems enquiry 12%; vascular examination 59%, pulses 46%; observations 31%; VTE assessment 73%
intervention: Clerking pro forma based on RCP guidance (with AMTS, VTE, ABPI, investigations and nil-by-mouth sections), junior doctor education and a named FY1 lead per cohort
cycle2_result: Sustained improvement in record keeping; observations recorded in 62% (significant increase); non-significant improvements in nil-by-mouth status and prior investigations
other_findings: At PDSA 1 (30 clerkings, 28 on the pro forma) most domains improved significantly (p <0.05), but observations were 42% and nil-by-mouth documentation fell. A later check of 23 acute-take clerkings not using the pro forma was as poor as baseline.
authors: Kentley J; Fox A; Taylor S; Hassan Y; Filipek A
citation: Kentley J, Fox A, Taylor S, Hassan Y, Filipek A. The use of a pro forma to improve quality in clerking vascular surgery patients. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2016;5(1):u210642.w4280. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u210642.w4280. PMID: 27418964.

title: Improving Mental Status Questionnaire (MSQ) completion on admission to the Acute Surgical Receiving Unit (ASRU), Ninewells Hospital, Dundee.
standard: Mental Status Questionnaire completed on admission for 95% of patients aged 75 or over (project target)
finding: MSQ completion 14.99% (16.6% and 13.3% in the two five-day periods); no patient had a formal delirium diagnosis despite a mean of 5.4 of 12 risk factors
change: Sticker listing all 10 MSQ questions in the admission document, with signage, email to junior doctors and advanced nurse practitioners briefing new staff
setting: Acute Surgical Receiving Unit, Ninewells Hospital, Dundee, tertiary centre
cycle1_result: MSQ completion 14.99% (16.6% and 13.3% in the two five-day periods); no patient had a formal delirium diagnosis despite a mean of 5.4 of 12 risk factors
intervention: Sticker listing all 10 MSQ questions in the admission document, with signage, email to junior doctors and advanced nurse practitioners briefing new staff
cycle2_result: Average MSQ completion 81.33%; 100% on two days; 40% on the first day
other_findings: Compliance dipped at the weekend and with junior doctor rotation; there was no clear pathway for patients with low MSQ scores.
authors: Okwemba S; Copeland L
citation: Okwemba S, Copeland L. Improving Mental Status Questionnaire (MSQ) completion on admission to the Acute Surgical Receiving Unit (ASRU), Ninewells Hospital, Dundee. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2014;3(1):u205217.w2159. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u205217.w2159. PMID: 27493742.

title: Improving bowel preparation for colonoscopy in a cost effective manner.
standard: JAG/BCSP: excellent or adequate bowel preparation in more than 90% of colonoscopies
finding: 490 (80%) adequate preparation; 118 (19%) inadequate; 14 (2.24%) needed repeat investigation; 100% PEG preparations
change: Patient information leaflets with diet and medication advice, algorithm-based choice of bowel preparation triaged by consultants, and cheaper postage in padded envelopes
setting: Endoscopy unit, University Hospital Llandough, Cardiff and Vale University Health Board
cycle1_result: 490 (80%) adequate preparation; 118 (19%) inadequate; 14 (2.24%) needed repeat investigation; 100% PEG preparations
intervention: Patient information leaflets with diet and medication advice, algorithm-based choice of bowel preparation triaged by consultants, and cheaper postage in padded envelopes
cycle2_result: 93 (93%) adequate preparation; 7% inadequate; no repeat investigations; PEG use 58.82%
other_findings: An interim re-audit of 873 patients at 3 months showed 83.5% adequate and 2.29% repeats. Estimated annual savings were £23,265 from postage, £12,000 from prescribing and about £150,000 from fewer repeat procedures.
authors: Gardezi SA; Tibbatts C
citation: Gardezi SA, Tibbatts C. Improving bowel preparation for colonoscopy in a cost effective manner. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2017;6(1):u204560.w5376. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u204560.w5376. PMID: 28607683.

title: Prevention of acute kidney injury through accurate fluid balance monitoring.
standard: Completion of six key fluid balance chart components (patient details, weight, running hourly input, 6-hourly input and output subtotals, 24-hour total); project aim of a 50% reduction in monthly AKI alerts
finding: Patient details 100%; weight 8%; running 1-hour input 80%; 6-hour input 83%; 6-hour urine output 36%; 24-hour balance 12%; mean 47 AKI alerts per month (October 2015 to January 2016)
change: Redesigned fluid balance chart, posters of correct and incorrect charts, handover scenario training, three-level e-learning modules, patient leaflets and regular feedback of AKI rates to junior doctors
setting: Acute orthopaedic trauma ward, regional trauma centre, North Bristol NHS Trust
cycle1_result: Patient details 100%; weight 8%; running 1-hour input 80%; 6-hour input 83%; 6-hour urine output 36%; 24-hour balance 12%; mean 47 AKI alerts per month (October 2015 to January 2016)
intervention: Redesigned fluid balance chart, posters of correct and incorrect charts, handover scenario training, three-level e-learning modules, patient leaflets and regular feedback of AKI rates to junior doctors
cycle2_result: Running 1-hour total 96%; 6-hourly output 68%; weight 16% (after peaking at 80%); 24-hour running total 32% (after peaking at 72%); monthly AKI alerts fell from 50 (January 2016) to 19 (November 2016), mean down 33% to 31 (P<0.001)
other_findings: An interim re-audit was done in March 2016. Weights and 24-hour totals fell back after early gains, and staff found adding up the 24-hour totals difficult.
authors: Davies A; Srivastava S; Seligman W; Motuel L; Deogan V; Ahmed S; Howells N
citation: Davies A, Srivastava S, Seligman W, Motuel L, Deogan V, Ahmed S, et al.. Prevention of acute kidney injury through accurate fluid balance monitoring. BMJ Open Qual. 2017;6(2):e000006. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2017-000006. PMID: 29435501.

title: A quality improvement project to improve the Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) sepsis bundle compliance rate in a large healthcare system.
standard: CMS sepsis bundle (SEP-1) compliance; aim to improve from 30% to 40% within 1 year
finding: Mean compliance 25.8% (monthly range 16-31%); baseline rate for SPC 28.5%.
change: Revised sepsis standardised clinical practice and system-wide education; computerised decision support to reflex-order repeat lactate and prompt lactate and blood cultures when antibiotics ordered; pharmacy made first-time IV antibiotic orders stat.
setting: 20 acute care hospitals, Banner Health system, Arizona
cycle1_result: Mean compliance 25.8% (monthly range 16-31%); baseline rate for SPC 28.5%.
intervention: Revised sepsis standardised clinical practice and system-wide education; computerised decision support to reflex-order repeat lactate and prompt lactate and blood cultures when antibiotics ordered; pharmacy made first-time IV antibiotic orders stat.
cycle2_result: Mean compliance 34.6% in the second 6 months (p<0.0001), peaking at 42%; 31.8% after CMS changed specifications in July 2016 (p<0.019 vs baseline).
other_findings: Most commonly missed elements were repeat lactate (30%), blood cultures (19%) and antibiotics (16%); the improvement was not sustained after the CMS specification change. Total denominator over 12 months was 1850 patients.
authors: Raschke RA; Groves RH; Khurana HS; Nikhanj N; Utter E; Hartling D; Stoffer B; Nunn K; Tryon S; Bruner M; Calleja M; Curry SC
citation: Raschke RA, Groves RH, Khurana HS, Nikhanj N, Utter E, Hartling D, et al.. A quality improvement project to improve the Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) sepsis bundle compliance rate in a large healthcare system. BMJ Open Qual. 2017;6(2):e000080. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2017-000080. PMID: 29450277.

title: Improving anticoagulation of patients with an implantable left ventricular assist device.
standard: Warfarin with target INR 2.5 (acceptable range 2.0 to 3.0); time in therapeutic range by Rosendaal method
finding: 0.38 INR measurements per patient-week; mean INR 2.46±0.59; time in therapeutic range 67.96%; 36 episodes out of range
change: Home point-of-care INR testing for all patients with results by email, a networked electronic INR and dosing database, and a dedicated daily VAD coordinator session for anticoagulation
setting: Transplant Unit, Royal Papworth Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Cambridge
cycle1_result: 0.38 INR measurements per patient-week; mean INR 2.46±0.59; time in therapeutic range 67.96%; 36 episodes out of range
intervention: Home point-of-care INR testing for all patients with results by email, a networked electronic INR and dosing database, and a dedicated daily VAD coordinator session for anticoagulation
cycle2_result: 1.24 INR measurements per patient-week; mean INR 2.48±0.6; time in therapeutic range 76.56% (not significant)
other_findings: Second cycle (January 2015): 0.9 measurements per patient-week (p=0.006) and 77.97% time in range. A small number of patients were out of range for long periods.
authors: Sage W; Gottiparthy A; Lincoln P; Tsui SSL; Pettit SJ
citation: Sage W, Gottiparthy A, Lincoln P, Tsui SSL, Pettit SJ. Improving anticoagulation of patients with an implantable left ventricular assist device. BMJ Open Qual. 2018;7(4):e000250. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2017-000250. PMID: 30306143.

title: Improving patient flow in a regional anaesthesia block room.
standard: Locally set targets: 90% of patients in block room 60 min before OR start; 90% arrive within 15 min of calling the surgical preparation unit; 90% enter OR within 10 min of scheduled start
finding: 31% arrived in the block room 60 min before OR start; 69% arrived within 15 min of the call; 52% entered OR within 10 min of scheduled start
change: Audit feedback to stakeholders, preparing flagged patients in the block room with a dedicated prep nurse, a structured OR-block room communication loop and consistent block room nursing staff
setting: Regional anaesthesia block room, University Hospital, London Health Sciences Centre, tertiary academic centre, London, Ontario
cycle1_result: 31% arrived in the block room 60 min before OR start; 69% arrived within 15 min of the call; 52% entered OR within 10 min of scheduled start
intervention: Audit feedback to stakeholders, preparing flagged patients in the block room with a dedicated prep nurse, a structured OR-block room communication loop and consistent block room nursing staff
cycle2_period: Re-measurement 1 month after PDSA cycles (project September 2016 to June 2017)
cycle2_result: 53% arrived 60 min before OR start (p=0.04); 98% within 15 min of the call (p<0.001); 65% entered OR on time (p=0.03)
other_findings: Two targets remained well below 90%. Day-to-day variation in case mix and staffing limited flow, and the work supported extra staffing and IT tracking tools.
authors: Brown B; Khemani E; Lin C; Armstrong K
citation: Brown B, Khemani E, Lin C, Armstrong K. Improving patient flow in a regional anaesthesia block room. BMJ Open Qual. 2019;8(2):e000346. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2018-000346. PMID: 31206045.

title: Quality improvement project aimed at improving the reliability of spontaneous awakening trials in a district general intensive care unit.
standard: Critical care guidelines recommending light sedation with a daily sedation hold (spontaneous awakening trial); project target 80% of eligible patients
finding: Median 47% of SAT-eligible patients received a sedation hold; mean RASS -2.3; 7 ventilated days and 10 unit days on average
change: Multidisciplinary sedation hold protocol based on the 'Wake up and breathe' guidelines, tested in PDSA cycles, with staff education, consultant prompting and a daily audit form
setting: 10-bed combined ICU/HDU, Hairmyres Hospital, NHS Lanarkshire, district general hospital
cycle1_result: Median 47% of SAT-eligible patients received a sedation hold; mean RASS -2.3; 7 ventilated days and 10 unit days on average
intervention: Multidisciplinary sedation hold protocol based on the 'Wake up and breathe' guidelines, tested in PDSA cycles, with staff education, consultant prompting and a daily audit form
cycle2_result: 96% of SAT-eligible patients received a sedation break; ventilation 5.5 days and unit stay 8 days; no adverse events
other_findings: During PDSA testing 65% then 79% received holds. Average RASS did not improve (-2.4), and medical staff were less aware of the protocol than nurses.
authors: Ferraioli D; Ferguson L; Carberry M
citation: Ferraioli D, Ferguson L, Carberry M. Quality improvement project aimed at improving the reliability of spontaneous awakening trials in a district general intensive care unit. BMJ Open Qual. 2019;8(2):e000518. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2018-000518. PMID: 31206059.

title: Optimizing Time to Antibiotic Administration in Children with Possible Febrile Neutropenia through Quality Improvement Methodologies.
standard: Time to antibiotic administration <60 minutes; aim >80% of eligible patients within 60 minutes
finding: Mean time to antibiotics 64 minutes; 59% received antibiotics in <60 minutes.
change: PDSA cycles: target of antibiotic order within 13 minutes with abnormality tracker, emails and audit and feedback; revised order set with antibiotic flagged urgent and pharmacy prioritisation; EHR change allowing antibiotic ordering before patient arrival using most recent weight.
setting: Pediatric emergency department, Oregon Health and Science University academic medical centre
cycle1_result: Mean time to antibiotics 64 minutes; 59% received antibiotics in <60 minutes.
intervention: PDSA cycles: target of antibiotic order within 13 minutes with abnormality tracker, emails and audit and feedback; revised order set with antibiotic flagged urgent and pharmacy prioritisation; EHR change allowing antibiotic ordering before patient arrival using most recent weight.
cycle2_result: Mean time to antibiotics 53 minutes; 84% received antibiotics in <60 minutes.
other_findings: Gains were sustained in the maintenance period (April 2016 to March 2017) with mean 44 minutes and 85% within 60 minutes; balancing measures (asthma bronchodilator and steroid times) did not worsen.
authors: Burns B; Hartenstein M; Lin A; Langley D; Burns E; Heilman J; Tanski M; Stork L; Ma OJ
citation: Burns B, Hartenstein M, Lin A, Langley D, Burns E, Heilman J, et al.. Optimizing Time to Antibiotic Administration in Children with Possible Febrile Neutropenia through Quality Improvement Methodologies. Pediatr Qual Saf. 2019;4(6):e236. doi:10.1097/pq9.0000000000000236. PMID: 32010862.

title: Improving Accuracy of Handoff by Implementing an Electronic Health Record-generated Tool: An Improvement Project in an Academic Neonatal Intensive Care Unit.
standard: Targets: handoff data accuracy 80%, incorrectly listed medications reduced (0% target), verbal handoff time reduced by 20%, user satisfaction up 1 point on a 5-point Likert scale
finding: Composite accuracy of 16 patient data points 51% (demographics 37%, medical data 66%); patients with incorrect or incomplete medication lists 51%.
change: EHR-generated structured handoff tool with autopopulated fields (Epic SmartPhrases), developed through PDSA cycles with stakeholder feedback, tutorials and a pilot; went live February 2019.
setting: Level 3 academic NICU (49 beds), University of California San Diego Jacobs Medical Center
cycle1_result: Composite accuracy of 16 patient data points 51% (demographics 37%, medical data 66%); patients with incorrect or incomplete medication lists 51%.
intervention: EHR-generated structured handoff tool with autopopulated fields (Epic SmartPhrases), developed through PDSA cycles with stakeholder feedback, tutorials and a pilot; went live February 2019.
cycle2_result: Composite accuracy 97% (demographics 100%, medical data 94%); incorrect medication lists 0%.
other_findings: Verbal handoff time did not change; user satisfaction appeared to increase (7 respondents per post-implementation survey). Handoffs were audited 4-5 times a month.
authors: Koo JK; Moyer L; Castello MA; Arain Y
citation: Koo JK, Moyer L, Castello MA, Arain Y. Improving Accuracy of Handoff by Implementing an Electronic Health Record-generated Tool: An Improvement Project in an Academic Neonatal Intensive Care Unit. Pediatr Qual Saf. 2020;5(4):e329. doi:10.1097/pq9.0000000000000329. PMID: 32766500.

title: Reducing redundant creatine kinase testing in cardiac injury.
standard: Choosing Wisely and cardiology society guidance that troponin alone is the biomarker of choice for cardiac injury; target 50% reduction in CK tests and CK-to-troponin ratio of one-third or less
finding: 47,556 CK tests (mean 3963 per month); CK-to-troponin ratio 0.91; 72.8% of CK tests coupled with troponin.
change: Revised institutional testing guidelines; CK removed from ED triage, cardiology admission, cardiovascular surgery and ICU order sets; academic detailing and education; unit-level comparative feedback by email; reduced default intervals for recurring CK tests.
setting: Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, large academic cardiac centre, Toronto
cycle1_result: 47,556 CK tests (mean 3963 per month); CK-to-troponin ratio 0.91; 72.8% of CK tests coupled with troponin.
intervention: Revised institutional testing guidelines; CK removed from ED triage, cardiology admission, cardiovascular surgery and ICU order sets; academic detailing and education; unit-level comparative feedback by email; reduced default intervals for recurring CK tests.
cycle2_result: 25,332 CK tests (mean 2111 per month), a 46.7% reduction (p<0.001); CK-to-troponin ratio 0.49; coupled tests 58.3% of CK orders.
other_findings: Troponin testing did not change; the reduction was sustained in January to March 2020 and projected annual savings were C$28,446. The 50% target was narrowly missed.
authors: Raza S; Amaral AC; Pang J; Moussa F; Shelton D; Notario L; Harrington H; Callum JL; Yip PM
citation: Raza S, Amaral AC, Pang J, Moussa F, Shelton D, Notario L, et al.. Reducing redundant creatine kinase testing in cardiac injury. BMJ Open Qual. 2020;9(4):e001182. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2020-001182. PMID: 33376105.

title: Implementation of a nutrition screening tool to improve nutritional status of children with cancer in Singapore's largest paediatric hospital.
standard: Universal nutrition screening within 24 hours of admission (JCI accreditation); aim for timely dietitian referral of high-risk children within 48 hours of admission
finding: 4 of 11 (36.4%) high-risk patients referred to the dietitian; 16 of 30 (53.3%) seen within 48 hours; median time to dietitian 3 days (IQR 1-14); malnutrition at admission 45 of 258 (17.4%).
change: Validated cancer-specific screening tool (SCAN) with nurse champion training; mandatory SCAN template in the EMR with auto-populated weights; direct dietitian self-referral from a work board flag.
setting: Paediatric oncology ward, KK Women's and Children's Hospital Cancer Centre, Singapore
cycle1_result: 4 of 11 (36.4%) high-risk patients referred to the dietitian; 16 of 30 (53.3%) seen within 48 hours; median time to dietitian 3 days (IQR 1-14); malnutrition at admission 45 of 258 (17.4%).
intervention: Validated cancer-specific screening tool (SCAN) with nurse champion training; mandatory SCAN template in the EMR with auto-populated weights; direct dietitian self-referral from a work board flag.
cycle2_result: 42 of 49 (85.7%) high-risk patients seen by the dietitian (p=0.005); 40 of 41 (97.6%) seen within 48 hours; median time to dietitian 1 day (p=0.010); malnutrition 17 of 260 (6.5%).
other_findings: Screening completion was 94.4% in PDSA cycle 1 but referral remained low (62.7%) until direct referral was introduced; early intervention was associated with better weight change at 3 months.
authors: Han WM; Koo JY; Lim YY; Iyer P; Ong C; Tong JW; Chan MY
citation: Han WM, Koo JY, Lim YY, Iyer P, Ong C, Tong JW, et al.. Implementation of a nutrition screening tool to improve nutritional status of children with cancer in Singapore's largest paediatric hospital. BMJ Open Qual. 2021;10(1):e000944. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2020-000944. PMID: 33707289.

title: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Reduce Blood Culture Contamination in the Neonatal Unit.
